title: Fantasy Football: The worst pick you can make in the final rounds of drafts in 2026
description: Fantasy football analyst Chris Allen wraps up his series detailing the worst picks of fantasy football drafts.
fullText:
Not to date myself, but I came up in a time when first-person shooter video games were picking up in popularity. I latched on to "Counter-Strike" during my first year of undergrad in 2001. The whole floor of my dorm was male engineers only. It was a perfect haven for LAN parties. While some of my classmates practiced with rifles, I tended toward the "spray and pray" options. My reasoning was simple:

If I fire enough bullets in the video game, I'm bound to hit somebody.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Football league for the 2026 NFL season

However, I (quickly) found a flaw in my plan. More ammo didn't necessarily equate to a stronger KDA ratio in the game. I was cannon fodder! Instead of flinging shells, controlled bursts and a coordinated approach were the right play — not my Leroy Jenkins impersonation. And as we get to the end of our drafts, that's how we should be approaching picks we think of as just throwaways.

Part III is here, the worst picks of Rounds 9-12. Go here for Part II of this series, the worst picks of Rounds 5-8. Here's also Part I, the worst picks of the first four rounds.

To be clear, I understand why we get looser with our play to finish filling out our rosters. First, we've (hopefully) got all the guys we really care about. Like when Josh Norris snagged De'Zhaun Stribling in our analysts league. No other pick earned higher praise. But I shrugged through clicking on Deebo Samuel Sr. about five rounds later. Because, in general, I know what to expect.

I bucketed the RBs and WRs by their end-of-season rank and averaged their PPR point totals. Two takeaways here. The first takes us back to the intro.

Yes, season-long output is dropping like a rock. Going from about the WR40 to the WR50 will cost you about 1.8 PPR PPG. Double that if you play in a deeper league and have to swim in the WR70 waters. But there's still SOME value. Since 2021, rushers in the RB73-78 range have averaged 3.2 weeks inside the top 48. That's a FLEX-level player for about 20% of the regular season at almost no cost to you. Hence, we're not just throwing darts to have fun. But the gap between the two lines holds the larger point.

Rushers generate about 40 fewer points of production than receivers with a similar rank. And the delta widens deeper into the draft. By the 67-72 tier, RB output falls to half of a receiver's. Accordingly, we can't apply the same threshold to calculate bust rates for both positions.

Using different limits for either RB or WR answered the range-appropriate question for this area of the draft. Whether or not they earned the bench slot is what will see us through a season filled with chaos. As the data suggested, we're only getting a few weeks out of them. But if you cluster enough good shots together, you're doing damage to the rest of the league. Or, put another way, the low boundary doesn't promise these guys were startable every week — it promises they were worth the stash.

Anyway, let's see what caused some of these guys to whiff on their ADP.

Seeing injuries as the main catalyst for a bust isn't anything new. And the severity carried similar ramifications as to how we treated them in fantasy. The average rusher missed 9.8 games, with receivers at 8.6. That's more than half of the fantasy season. However, the absence didn't completely erode the value for one of the positions.

RBs who were earning some touches within their offense prior to injury mostly returned to form upon their return. Sure, their opportunities as receivers fell by 24.1%. But if they got money touches before, those duties were still available to them. However, it was a different story for WRs.

Despite still being on the field, receiver workloads took a tumble. As it requires synchronicity between the QB and WR, any break in their rhythm to practice timing should have a downstream effect. As such, I'll be more willing to cycle through late-round receivers who get hurt than rushers in the future. But we should still pay more attention to the busts who stayed healthy all year.

A few names to consider when looking at this chart: Kimani Vidal, Zamir White and Sean Tucker. All rookies who piqued the interest of fantasy gamers, but not their own coordinators. As they got stuck behind established starters, there wasn't a foothold to accumulate more touches. And from Jalen Reagor in 2021 to Darnell Mooney in 2023, the instant a role player faced greater talent, their production waned. So, with these profiles in mind, let's see who we should be avoiding to close out our drafts.

If I had to guess, at first, Tyler Allgeier leaving the Falcons brought joy to both fans of Allgeier and Bijan Robinson.

Tyler Allgeier opens up the scoring with authority 😤

BUFvsATL on ESPN
Stream on @NFLPlus and ESPN App pic.twitter.com/1zwXODTz1P

In another universe, the former fifth-rounder is still in Atlanta as the lead back. We don't consider Allgeier to be a "fantasy vulture." More importantly, we recognize him for the above-average runner that he's shown to be in small samples. Even though Robinson relegated him to be the early-down option, Allgeier (mostly) kept up with the guy almost two years younger than him.

(Early-Down) Rushing Success Rate: 44.9% (Allgeier), 47.9%

Adj. Yards after Contact per Att.: 3.4, 4.4

Explosive Play Rate: 9.1%, 9.5%

There's a reason why the two Atlanta RBs split the goal-line work. And it wasn't just because Arthur Smith wanted to troll us. An expanded role would do everybody good. However, Allgeier's landing spot couldn't have been worse.

(2025) Rushing Plays per Game: 21.5, 32nd

Offensive Points per Game: 16.7, 20th

Arizona was in the bottom half of the league in almost every metric. After Jacoby Brissett took over, they scored just five TDs on the ground. Greg Dortch scored one. Brissett took another in himself. Combined with the Cardinals' selection of Jeremiyah Love in the first round, Allgeier's environment and direct competition make him an avoid.

I understand why drafters would let nostalgia take over and click on Alvin Kamara in the late rounds.

Tyler Shough hands one off to Alvin Kamara pic.twitter.com/jpTslp91dp

Everybody remembers Kamara's Christmas gift to fantasy managers back in 2020. But even since then, his usage as a receiver has kept us coming back. It didn't matter when New Orleans added Mark Ingram to take on the short-yardage carries. The duo was one of the best in the league. Jamaal Williams came down from Detroit in '23. Kamara was still the RB to target in NOLA. His 5.8 targets per game kept his fantasy value afloat. But 2025 brought a sudden change to the offense.

2021: 46.5% (Route Rate), 14.1% (Target Share)

While we've praised Kellen Moore for his progressive approach to play-calling, the target distribution (specifically to RBs) has favored WRs. Going back to 2019, Austin Ekeler is the only rusher to average more than five targets per game with Moore as his coach or coordinator. Ezekiel Elliott came close in 2020 (4.7). Regardless, rushers primarily do what their designation suggests.

Yes, it doesn't help that Kamara is 31 years old and dealing with an MCL sprain already. Plus, Travis Etienne signed on over the offseason to take the lead. But when combined with the scheme change, the prospect of drafting Kamara becomes even more daunting.

If you've been paying attention to the Browns' training camp, you'll know that I'm not mentioning Denzel Boston because he lacks any talent.

Denzel Boston Is Looking Like the NFL’s BEST Rookie WR in Training Camp So Far...😳 pic.twitter.com/s4qa5SwUlj

At 6'4"-215lbs, the Washington product looks every bit the WR1 archetype needed in Cleveland. Cedric Tillman is off the team. Jerry Jeudy could be a cap casualty during the '27 offseason. All roads point to Boston becoming a larger force within the passing game. However, if preseason was any indication, there's still more he has to overcome.

Malachi Corley: 15.4% (Target Share)

Of course, August is just a dress rehearsal. Talent should win out (right?). But we can all agree these four pass-catchers should factor into the weekly rotation. And then there's Harold Fannin Jr. Oh wait, I forgot about a deep shot or two to Isaiah Bond, too. That's six options right there without even naming Boston. Now, let's consider their QB.

Deshaun Watson in first practice since being named starting QB

(via @atlTVnews) pic.twitter.com/00Xpbr5T6c

Even in August, Deshaun Watson was averaging 5.4 air yards per attempt. And he still took a sack and caused two turnovers. I'll check back in on Boston next year.

I have the same feelings about Keenan Allen that I do about Kamara.

Will you be drafting Keenan Allen in fantasy this season? pic.twitter.com/OJUBAgl92T

Allen was Amon-Ra St. Brown before the Sun God ascended into our lives. The Chargers' long-time WR1 was the epitome of a "set-it-and-forget-it" player in PPR leagues. But Father Time has been knocking on his door for a while.

2023 (Age: 31): 24.4% (Target Rate), 30.5% (Air Yard Share), 2.37 (YPRR)

From L.A. to Chicago and back, Allen's route-running skills never left. Coupled with his short-area aDOT, he never lacked for looks. But what he can do with them has dwindled. His YAC per reception has steadily declined (3.7 to 2.9). And don't expect to see too many explosives.

We're already skeptical about the Colts offense. That's why just two skill players have early-round price tags. And one is an RB. If the potential for the offense to crater exists, let's not add risk by taking a receiver from that same team in the twilight of their career.

title: Can Commanders Wr Antonio Williams have a Scary Terry-like rookie year? - Daily Slop
description: The talented young receiver is perfectly positioned to exceed expectations from Day 1
fullText:
Editor's note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

That should give Jones flexibility in who wears the green dot while still allowing Styles to grow into the role without forcing every part of the defense onto him at once.

The bigger takeaway is how quickly Washington appears willing to trust him. There were always questions about how much Styles would be asked to handle as a rookie, especially in a defense with this many moving parts. The answer is becoming pretty clear. Washington didn't draft him seventh overall just to make plays. They drafted him to become one of the pieces the defense can eventually revolve around, and giving him a hand in directing it before his first regular-season snap shows they may already be treating him that way.

It's worth pointing out that Washington's current mashup of offensive linemen was not the plan the team had in mind. In a perfect world, Tunsil would remain the left tackle, Allegretti would have been on the field for most of camp and the duo of Sam Cosmi and Josh Conerly would have continued building their chemistry together on the right side. The only position that would have been undecided was left guard, but the team felt like it was in a good spot with either Coleman or Chris Paul.

But Tunsil's injury changed all that. The team likes what it has with Coleman at tackle, but that move affected the depth at guard. The uncertainty at guard put a brighter spotlight on the center position, which was already going through some flux with Allegretti's injury.

That's a lot of uncertainty for a position at which Commanders need to be solid this season, but the team is looking at the situation with optimism.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Antonio Williams – Commanders WR

The Washington Commanders' wide receiver room looks strong. There are some proven performers and also some reclamation projects who could improve within David Blough's system if everything goes well.

There is also Antonio Williams.

The third-round rookie wideout was projected as a first-rounder before a disappointing final college campaign with the Clemson Tigers. Williams has the talent, and the Commanders believe there is something that could be a major asset.

Based on the impression made over the summer, he's got a chance to feature as part of a trio with Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs.

Williams is a slick route runner who knows how to separate. He's got assured hands, can make things happen after the catch, and now has a chip on his shoulder after being overlooked until No. 71 overall in the draft.

McLaurin and Diggs will lead the charge. But don't be surprised if Williams becomes a surprise most don't see coming.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

The Commanders have dealt with multiple injuries over the past month, but there was some good news from Quinn: many of these players are working their way back to practice.

Quinn started the press conference by announcing that Allegretti, Marcus Mariota, Daron Payne, Jordan Magee and Ben Sinnott would be back at practice. Mariota's return is more of an insurance policy for Daniels, but players like Allegretti, Payne and the rest are either starters or will get significant playing time. Their returns provide them with valuable reps to prepare for the team's Week 1 road game against the Philadelphia Eagles.

Trey Amos, however, was not among the players who returned to practice, as he was placed on Injured Reserve earlier in the day. Amos will now have to miss at least the first four games of the season nursing an ankle injury he suffered in camp.

Outside linebacker Odafe Oweh was also not among the players returning to practice, but Quinn said the team is "feeling good" about his progress. "We're thrilled that he's making this kind of progress to get ready."

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Dan Quinn said Odafe Oweh is expected to return to practice next week. Whether that happens remains to be seen, but losing Oweh for Week 1 against the Eagles would be a major blow.

Jean-Baptiste has had the most complicated path of anyone in Washington's edge room. A seventh-round pick out of Notre Dame in Peters' first draft class in 2024, he spent most of his first two seasons either on injured reserve or playing limited rotational snaps behind a deep depth chart. A torn pectoral in 2025 cost him most of the year — he played just three games. But he came back healthy this spring, posted a 75.5 overall PFF grade across his limited 2025 snaps — with a 71.2 run-defense grade that ranked as one of the better marks among Washington's edge defenders — and has been one of the more consistent veterans in camp this August.

His career line is modest: 19 tackles and two sacks across 15 games. But the run defense and the effort level have never been the question. Against an Eagles offensive line that will likely try to establish the run early, Jean-Baptiste's physicality and gap discipline make him a useful early-down piece if Oweh can't go.

Blough spent one year in Minnesota learning coach Kevin O'Connell's offense and was on Detroit's practice squad in 2023 under coordinator Ben Johnson. Blough was influenced by Johnson in particular and will use a lot of play-action passes, more snaps from under center and far less no-huddle than Washington used under Kliff Kingsbury the past two years. They will retain some elements of Kingsbury's system — some run-pass option. Blough also could mimic Johnson when it comes to trickery and creativity. — John Keim

Key stat: Last season (with Blough as assistant quarterbacks coach and Kingsbury as offensive coordinator), the Commanders rushed on 61.4% of their red zone plays, the highest rate in the NFL. — ESPN Research

It is basically impossible to make LSU football look sympathetic in 2026. Jayden Daniels did it.

Adam Peters signed four 32 year olds, a 31 year old, and two 30 year olds in August alone.

Last year the Commanders went 0-3 in the preseason, finishing with a 30-3 loss to the Ravens, and then went 5-12 (in honor of Jayden Daniels). This year they went 1-2 in the preseason, with their win being against a Dolphins team that is not even trying to look like they're trying, and finished with a 41-3 loss to the Ravens.

Their weak OL is already depleted. LT Laremy Tunsil is out for most of the year, and C Nick Allegretti got hurt on day one of camp and hasn't practiced since.

The Commanders have said that they have no plans to bring back the old Redskins name or logo, but last week started selling merchandise with the Redskins name and (part of the) logo. It sold out in two days.

Most teams get better as training camp progresses. Washington got off on the wrong foot and went downhill from there.

Dallas fans are nervous about their first two games against the Giants & Commanders

Week 2 vs Washington Commanders

It may seem a bit crazy to list a Week 2 matchup as a must-win, but this game absolutely falls into that category for the Cowboys. Dallas opens up the season with two divisional matchups in a row, traveling to New York to take on the Giants in Week 1 before returning home to host the Commanders.

While Dallas has dominated the rivalry with the Giants in recent memory, this matchup will be much more difficult than years past. New York undoubtedly got better this offseason, and emotions will be running high as John Harbaugh makes his debut as the team's new head coach. Dallas is favored and very well could win the game, but there is a real possibility they walk out of New York 0-1.

If that happens, the Week 2 matchup against the Commanders becomes a clear must-win. Dropping to 0-2 with both losses coming to division opponents could nearly sink your season two weeks in.

Declan Doyle, OC, Baltimore Ravens

Sean Mannion, OC, Philadelphia Eagles

The Commanders (Jayden Daniels), Ravens (Lamar Jackson) and Eagles (Jalen Hurts) have three successful quarterbacks who have thrived working out of the shotgun or pistol and made a meaningful impact moving the ball with their legs on designed quarterback runs. And to some extent, those three teams are going to ask their quarterbacks to do something different in 2026 by operating from under center.

It's a big bet by three teams with quarterbacks who have already proved themselves as successful without needing to go under center very often. If those bets work out, Blough, Doyle and Mannion could be in line to earn head-coaching consideration as early as next offseason. If not, well, the world isn't very forgiving to young playcallers.

The 49ers are already in the air aboard their 16-hour flight to Melbourne, Australia, for a game against the Rams that won't kick off for another seven and a half days. They want plenty of time to adjust to Melbourne time after the longest road trip in NFL history.

The Rams are taking a very different approach.

Although Rams coach Sean McVay has declined to discuss the team's travel plans, they're reportedly leaving on Wednesday, September 9, which will mean landing less than 24 hours before kickoff: The game kicks off at 8:35 p.m. Eastern on Thursday, September 10, which is 10:35 a.m. on Friday, September 11, in Melbourne.

The Rams think delaying international travel for as long as possible the smart approach, and there's some precedent to suggest they're right: Last year the Rams didn't arrive in London for their game against the Jaguars until the day before, and they proceeded to destroy the Jaguars, who have long-established London travel plans of arriving days in advance.

title: Flamengo beat Mirassol and close in on Palmeiras

fullText:
Another Rubro-Negro celebration at the MaracanãCredits: Gilvan de Souza / Flamengo

In a postponed match from the 4th round of the Brasileirão Série A, Flamengo defeated Mirassol 2-0 on Wednesday night (2) at the Maracanã and reached 51 points in 25 matches. The team is now just one point behind leaders Palmeiras, who have played the same number of games. Carrascal and Paquetá scored Flamengo's goals.

With the result, Mirassol remained on 25 points and stayed out of the relegation zone by the slimmest of margins: they are 16th, with the same number of points, the same goal difference, and the same goals scored as Vasco, staying ahead of the Rio club because of the head-to-head record.

More than 60,000 people were at the Maracanã to watch Flamengo beat Mirassol 2-0.

The match was postponed from the 4th round because of Flamengo's participation in the Recopa Sudamericana final against Lanús of Argentina. The change gave the team more time to prepare for the second leg of the continental decider, which was played at the Maracanã.

On that occasion, the Argentine side won the title, with an aggregate score of 4-2 over the two final matches.

title: Satou Sabally ruled out for rest of 2026 WNBA season with head injury
description: A head injury will hold Liberty star Satou Sabally out for the remainder of the 2026 WNBA season. Here's what we know.
fullText:
New York Liberty forward Satou Sabally is out for the rest of the WNBA season.

On Thursday, the franchise announced Sabally will miss the remainder of the season after suffering head injury in June.

In August, the team shared she would temporarily leave the team to focus on her recovery.

"She's gonna be away from the team for a little bit. It's her second significant head injury in the past 12 months," Liberty head coach Chris Demarco said on Aug. 13. "As with all our players, health will always be the focus. We look forward to getting her back. She's just taking some time right now."

On Aug. 12, Sabally's injury designation was changed from concussion protocol to "head."

On June 23, during a game against the Las Vegas Aces, Sabally exited the matchup early. With 5:31 remaining in the first quarter, the Liberty star was elbowed in the face by Aces forward NaLyssa Smith as they competed for a rebound. Sabally, who was called for a loose-ball foul on the play, fell to the ground, removed her glasses and rubbed her head. She eventually got to her feet under her own power.

Sabally was subbed out and went to the bench. She returned to action at the start of the second quarter and played for nearly four minutes before checking back out. Sabally did not come back to the court. She played eight minutes, finishing with one assist and one block.

Sabally played 13 games for New York, starting five matchups. She averaged 10.4 points, 2.8 rebounds and 1.9 assists, while shooting 45.9% from the floor and 38.5% from the 3-point line.

Sabally has a history of concussions.

She suffered a concussion in Game 3 of the 2025 WNBA Finals while competing for the Phoenix Mercury after her head made contact with Aces forward Kierstan Bell's knee, trying to corral an offensive rebound. The injury ended Sabally's season early. During the offseason, she missed the second season of Unrivaled while dealing with lingering concussion symptoms.

Sabally didn't play in the Liberty's two preseason games due to reconditioning. She then missed the first four games of the season with a cyst, delaying her Liberty debut until May 21. Sabally was also sidelined on May 27 in the Liberty's 84-74 win over the Mercury with an illness.

title: The Athletic’s Findings From Dianna Russini-Mike Vrabel Affair Investigation Are a Nothing Burger That’ll Disappoint NFL Fans
description: On Thursday, The Athletic released its findings from the investigation into Dianna Russini’s unprofessional relationship with New England Patriots head […]
fullText:
On Thursday, The Athletic released its findings from the investigation into Dianna Russini's unprofessional relationship with New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel, and it is more about covering the outlet's butt when it comes to the news she covered for them instead of delving into whether she had more inappropriate relationships with sources.

One of the biggest stories in the NFL this spring actually came off the field and had nothing to do with one of the league's athletes. Instead, fans were captivated by an apparent affair that was happening between the popular insider and veteran coach.

While Russini is no longer with The Athletic, the outlet still did an internal investigation into her relationship with the coach and released some of the details from it today. However, the findings from the inquiry won't be what NFL fans will be looking for. Instead, The Athletic focused on whether her work for them was affected by her relationship with the coach.

The Athletic's editorial director for standards and editorial quality, Mike Semel, reviewed 903 stories and 77 videos published on The Athletic's site that Russini either authored or was a contributor to. He also spoke with 14 staffers who had worked with Russini.

While the report admits her conduct was not up to standards, as she never informed her bosses about the relationship and/or got in front of the situation when the New York Post's Page Six broke the news, it found limited evidence that she favored Vrabel in her content for The Athletic.

"Most of what Russini wrote about Vrabel or the Patriots was transactional and newsy," Semel wrote. "In addition, I've not found a clear link to conclude that Russini used her platform to promote Vrabel or help his teams during her time at The Athletic."

While that is certainly good for Russini and backs her claims that the relationship did not affect the content she created as an insider, the report doesn't answer two major questions: How long has this relationship been going on, and did she have any other unprofessional associations with sources?

In the five-month-long investigation, they did not dig deeper into how things went from professional to personal, and Semel purposely did not investigate Russini's personal conduct because she was no longer an employee of the company. However, he did add in his report, "The appearances surrounding her relationship with Vrabel undermine our audience's confidence in her impartiality."

In the end, The Athletic wanted to make sure Russini's work didn't specifically favor the Patriots and Vrabel. It unsurprisingly did not. However, for fans hoping to get more depth on if she used more inappropriate tactics to build her infrastructure of sources or how serious the relationship was, the report is a nothingburger.

title: NL East division will be decided this weekend
description: The NL East division features 2 of baseball's best teams.
fullText:
MLB's NL East race enters a pivotal stretch this weekend as the division-leading Atlanta Braves head into Philadelphia with a chance to stretch their lead to a commanding eight games. However, if things go poorly for Atlanta, that lead could vanish entirely when the Braves take on the Phillies in a four-game series that kicks off tonight at Citizens Bank Park.

The Braves, sitting at 83-57, hold a four-game edge atop the division over a surging Phillies squad that has won six of its last seven games and 15 of its last 18. A sweep by Philadelphia would pull the two teams level at the top of the NL East heading into the season's final stretch.

MORE: Guardians pitcher has career night in crucial battle for AL Wild Card spot

Jun 4, 2026; Cumberland, Georgia, USA; Atlanta Braves pitcher Chris Sale (51) looks on during the first inning against the Toronto Blue Jays at Truist Park. Mandatory Credit: Mady Mertens-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

The series opens with a marquee pitching matchup. Chris Sale, 37, takes the mound for Atlanta. The 2024 Cy Young winner has racked up 13 wins this season with a sparkling 2.06 ERA, and he struck out 11 batters in a 1-0 complete-game shutout of the Los Angeles Dodgers in his most recent start on Thursday.

Countering him is Philadelphia's Christopher Sanchez, who reached the 200-strikeout mark for the second consecutive season on Saturday. Sanchez struck out eight over seven innings and allowed just two hits in a 4-2 win over the Los Angeles Angels, underscoring why he's been one of the National League's most reliable arms this year.

MORE: Nationals' rookie duo makes MLB history Tuesday night

Beyond the division race, the Phillies (79-61) are also sitting comfortably atop the NL Wild Card standings, holding a 5.5-game cushion. A strong showing against Atlanta this weekend would let Philadelphia chase two goals at once: closing the division gap while further cementing their postseason position.

The two clubs are slated to meet just once more this season, in a three-game series in mid-September, meaning this weekend's four games at Citizens Bank Park could go a long way toward deciding who controls the NL East down the stretch.

title: Tua Tagovailoa's wife clears up burner account controversy
description: Falcons QB was accused of having a burner account after commenting on his own post
fullText:
NFL athletes face a level of scrutiny that most people can't even imagine. We analyze literally everything they do, oftentimes holding them to a standard that even some high-ranking politicians could never live up to. When you play quarterback, that scrutiny is ratcheted way up.

Falcons quarterback Tua Tagovailoa has been under the microscope since his time at Alabama, but he found himself facing burner account allegations after he appeared to comment on his own Instagram post.

"We're so proud of you," Tagovailoa appeared to write about himself under his own post (see below).

I’m going to start doing this in the comments of all my videos. pic.twitter.com/6rVd9lljN6

Fans got a good laugh out of the comment, but Tagovailoa's wife clarified that she was the one to accidentally post the loving message from Tua's IG account. She posted another comment explaining her mistake and pointing out that Tagovailoa has never run his own social media accounts.

"No burner account! I was busy with the kids this morning and forgot to switch back to my account. He's busy at work as he's said he doesn't have social media and I post on his behalf! Will pay more attention next time."

As funny as it was to imagine Tagovailoa commenting about himself from a burner account, we believe his wife was 100 percent telling the truth. The Falcons quarterback is likely more concerned with winning the starting job in his battle against Michael Penix Jr.

title: Dodgers considering huge Shohei Ohtani decision that would likely end MVP bid
description: This would be a massive decision for the Dodgers with the two-way superstar.
fullText:
Dodgers considering huge Shohei Ohtani decision that would likely end MVP bid originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The vibes around the Los Angeles Dodgers right now aren't the greatest. While they're likely still the World Series favorites due to the superteam they've assembled, the offense is struggling, and now Shohei Ohtani doesn't look right.

He was clearly not 100% during the Dodgers' loss to the St. Louis Cardinals on Wednesday. That should have Dodgers fans worried. Dave Roberts echoed that concern, saying the team is considering a major decision with Ohtani.

According to Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic, the Dodgers shutting down Ohtani from pitching for the rest of the season is "on the table." Not only would this be a blow to the Dodgers' postseason chances, but it would likely end Ohtani's MVP bid.

"Dave Roberts said the possibility of shutting down Shohei Ohtani as a pitcher for the season is on the table, but the Dodgers aren't to the point yet where they have to or will make that decision," Ardaya reports.

While the Dodgers have not made the decision to shut Ohtani down from pitching again this season, the fact that it's under consideration is a bad sign.

It's clear he isn't 100% right now, and with under a month to go before the postseason begins, the Dodgers might be better off playing it as safe as possible with Ohtani.

He was shut down from returning to the mound not too long ago, and now a full-blown shutdown is potentially in play.

MORE: Kevin McGonigle is runaway favorite to win AL Rookie of the Year for Tigers

Such a decision would very likely end his 2026 MVP bid. As good as he has been, with 6.5 bWAR between his hitting and pitching value with 30 homers, a .906 OPS and a 1.79 ERA in 85.2 innings, he's currently having a rough end to 2026.

He was the first-half MVP by a considerable margin, but now there is a good chance that Ohtani loses the NL MVP award to Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs.

That becomes all the more likely if Ohtani cannot return to the mound, which seems fairly likely considering the Dodgers shutting him down is "on the table" right now, according to Roberts.

If they do shut him down, then Ohtani's MVP bid would likely end, which would be a huge shame considering a fourth-straight MVP award seemed like a lock this season back in July.

fullText:
As graduates of an online training course gather from across the continent, the consensus is overwhelming: computers and saving animals go together

On a bitingly cold night in Lapalala Wilderness nature reserve in South Africa’s Limpopo province, Duncan Kanyakera watches as instructor Jacques Viljoen deploys a thermal drone in search of a lone cheetah. Once the drone has disappeared into the inky sky, Kanyakera, from Tsavo in Kenya, and 20 other conservation professionals from across Africa turn their attention to the open-air screen in anticipation.

Many of the students – from 11 African countries as far flung as Benin, Liberia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar – witnessing the demonstration have earned their places at Lapalala after performing well on an online training programme for protected area technicians (PAT) run by the Connected Conservation Foundation (CCF). Also on the course, are five members of Peace Parks staff in training.

“Data and technology are critical to modern conservation,” says CCF’s Sophie Maxwell. “Cameras and collars and software like EarthRanger have transformed the fight against poaching … But then an elephant knocks over a pole and you are back to square one.”

Since 2015, the CCF has installed state-of-the-art tech systems in parks across Africa with remarkable success, helping to protect nearly 10m hectares (25m acres). “Parks with tech solutions are safer and more biodiverse and they have better relationships with communities,” says Maxwell.

Over the years, the CCF has “identified a critical gap”, says Carien Soldatos who oversees the PAT training programme: “Tech is fantastic, but it all depends on having trained technicians on the ground. Without people who know how to use, repair and maintain them, the fanciest gizmos in the world aren’t much use.” While there are such people in some parks, they are sorely lacking in many parts of Africa.

After searching everywhere for a tech course aimed at conservation professionals, the CCF decided to create its own. Their 10-module course, which launched in July 2025, was a global first. In the first year, 680 people from all over the world finished at least one module. Those who completed all 10 modules were invited to interviews, with the top 16 chosen to attend the practical component at Lapalala.

In less than 10 minutes, the heat sensor technology in the drone launched by Viljoen locates the cheetah resting with her cubs. Once he has locked its location, the operator sends a pin to the park’s on-duty field rangers, who rush to the scene. “I was stunned,” says Kanyakera. “There was no moon and the cheetah was miles away from us. But we could see exactly what was happening as the rangers got out of their vehicle and checked up on her.”

Kanyakera, who works for the Taita Taveta Wildlife Conservancies Association (TTWCA) to support a network of 35 conservancies and ranches in Kenya’s vast Tsavo landscape, recognised immediately how handy a drone would be back home. Human-wildlife conflict is a challenge in Tsavo: “If an elephant gets into a corn field, it causes havoc,” he says. “And then you have the problem of humans retaliating.”

The aim, says Kanyakera, is to keep humans and animals apart via designated wildlife corridors. But this gets tricky in the dry season when animals and humans alike are drawn towards water. Currently, if Kanyakera gets reports of an elephant near a village, he has to first work out where the elephant is and which direction it is moving in, before deploying rangers to intervene. This can take hours.

“With a drone, we could find the elephant in minutes,” he says. “The noise of the drone alone would probably be enough to scare the animal off. And if that doesn’t work, I can deploy rangers much more accurately.”

While a night-vision drone is the most exciting item on Kanyakera’s Christmas list, the course has also shown him how simple changes could drastically improve the tech “stack” back in Tsavo. This has a lot to do with the course design, explains Maxwell: “Each day, they build a new element of the stack,” she says, “before breaking it down at the end of each day and building it again the next morning to add another layer. It’s all about building muscle memory.”

And it seems to be working. “As soon as I get home, I’ll reconfigure our camera traps to make the most of AI,” says Kanyakera who also has his sights set on re-equipping the ops room in Tsavo. “In the past, we would just Google and make a decision. Now I know so much more, I can target what I really want. The learnings from this course can make a big difference to the people and animals of Tsavo.”

The course – which featured guest lectures and practicals from nine experts on topics including connectivity, communication, power systems, monitoring sensors, hardware integration and GIS visualisation tools – is having an impact far beyond Tsavo.

Effort Zivengwa, who works at the Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority head office in Harare, is part of a tech team responsible for 11 national parks. “We were content with what we were doing,” he says. “But, after completing this course, I think we have to do more. We are already using EarthRanger and we do have sensors, but they are not integrated.

“We have park headquarters and lodges that don’t have internet access,” he adds. “Using point-to-point internet can fix that problem easily.” The learning module on solar power further shifted his understanding of what is possible. “We have a lot of remote stations,” he says. “But the sun shines everywhere.”

Mabel Nokhuthula Piki, who teaches wildlife monitoring skills at the Chinhoyi University of Technology in central Zimbabwe, has also found the course empowering. “My students didn’t comprehend that tech was important. They couldn’t get the link between saving animals and computers. But now I am going to change their minds,” she says. “It is impossible to understand the value of tech until you have seen it.”

The CCF is planning to run a second practical course with another batch of students in the first quarter of 2027. What is more, says Soldatos, “we will be supporting five participants from the first course with internships and/or hardware donations”. The lucky five have not yet been chosen, but Kanyakera, Zivengwa and Piki are all in the running.

title: John Lewis to launch YouTube chatshow to improve AI search results
description: Department store chain’s Gift List ‘vodcast’ will be hosted by TV presenter Angela...
fullText:
Department store chain’s Gift List ‘vodcast’ will be hosted by TV presenter Angela Scanlon

John Lewis is launching an online chatshow and social media studio to help make itself and its products more visible to chatbots and more prominent in AI search results.

The department store chain’s Gift List “vodcast” hosted by the TV presenter Angela Scanlon will air on YouTube with clips disseminated via other social media channels and comes after the success of its sister chain Waitrose’s Dish podcast.

The premise is guests discussing good and bad presents they have given and received, with the broadcaster Louis Theroux appearing on the first show. There will be six episodes running up to Christmas, with more planned if the series takes off.

Shoppers are increasingly influenced by the likes of ChatGPT and Gemini to find and recommend products and also by information on social media such as Instagram and TikTok. The AI large language models tend to prioritise third-party advice and live content when formulating their responses, which is forcing retailers to change their marketing plans.

The department store’s outgoing boss, Peter Ruis, said that a year ago just 0.3% of its customers were searching for products via AI large language models such as ChatGPT, but that had already risen to 2.5%, and usage was growing exponentially with all ages using the technology.

Being able to rapidly respond to trends and interests with clips of influencers or experts filmed for social media – such as the opening of the British Museum’s Bayeux tapestry exhibition, which is expected to spur an interest in cross stitching, or the launch of the Harry Potter TV series before Christmas – has become just as important as the group’s festive TV ad or its ‘never knowingly undersold’ price pledge.

Ruis, who departs John Lewis this weekend after almost three years as managing director, said John Lewis had to move with the times as it faced an economy which was “a bit swirly”.

He said the chancellor’s budget announcements next month would come at a “critical period” for retailers and he wanted to see more help on business rates.

Ruis said strong trading this week and a string of recent innovations, including modernised cafes and sports departments as well as the social media push and a recent “toy boom”, made him optimistic about the run-up to Christmas.

Details of John Lewis’s half-year figures will be released next week. Ruis said it had been a “summer of winners and losers” but indicated there was now “decent momentum” as shoppers still had money to spend.

The chain rang up record sales of garden furniture, fans and air conditioning over the summer but Ruis said it was not yet clear if the “Burnham bounce” over the summer would last. “People are not going to splurge when you have got inflation swirling,” he said.

“It’s not an easy economy. It’s not easy for customers and inflation is kicking in and the fuel pump is costing people a lot of money.”

Ruis last month announced his abrupt departure, saying he was going to “pursue new projects”. He gave no further clue on his future plans on Thursday but said there was “no misalignment” on strategy with John Lewis’s relatively new chair, Jason Tarry.

“We are getting things done at pace,” Ruis said, adding there was “never a good time” to leave but it was “far better to leave a winning team at the top of its game and all that excitement with events next year to unveil, rather than finishing bottom of the league and running out of the door”.

Ruis insisted his departure did not indicate that he had lost hope in the future of John Lewis, saying it was not a traditional department store reliant on fashion and beauty like Harvey Nichols, which was bought out of administration by Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group last month.

He said John Lewis sold a third of all UK prams and pushchairs, garden furniture and the latest technology and “this is not stuff Harvey Nichols can sell”.

fullText:
Semi-conductor giant bets that support for open AI models could offset potential slowdown in demand for chips

Nvidia will buy the popular developer platform Hugging Face for nearly $13bn, betting that support for ⁠open AI models could offset a potential slowdown in demand for the semiconductor giant’s chips.

Shares ⁠in Nvidia were ⁠slightly lower ​after the $12.93bn (£9.57bn) deal – which ranks among its biggest ever – was announced for the database of AI models on Thursday.

The New York-based startup Hugging Face, which is backed by Intel, Advanced Micro Devices and Amazon, was founded in 2016 by the French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf.

The chipmaker is already a major open AI player in the US with ⁠its widely used Nemotron model and vocal support for the technology.

Acquiring Hugging Face will give it direct access to a platform developers use to ⁠collaborate, test and share tools, potentially providing insight and data that could help it narrow the ​technology gap with top American and ‌Chinese labs.

Demand for open-weight models ‌has surged from businesses balking at the steep bill of deploying the technology. Chinese companies ‌such as DeepSeek and Z.ai have emerged as crucial players with models that can match the best from the US in tasks including generating computer code at a lower cost.

There are fears that some US firms could become reliant on Beijing’s models even as both countries race to dominate a technology they see as crucial to their future.

“Hugging ‌Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem,” said Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, adding that his company’s chips would not be required to ​build on or deploy through Hugging Face.

Under the deal, Nvidia will pay about $11.9bn to Hugging Face investors, while offering an equity-based retention programme of up to $1bn for employees who join Nvidia.

For Nvidia, building up its open source business may help it cushion a demand slowdown from customers such as ⁠Meta, OpenAI and Microsoft, which are developing their own AI chips to cut reliance ​on its costly and ​supply constrained processors.

Hugging Face has also been ​in the news recently after a hack by rogue AI agents that ​escaped OpenAI’s testing ‌environment. Beyond hosting AI ​models, it offers datasets, ​software libraries and cloud services used to build and deploy AI applications.

fullText:
Tech company submits to controversial Trump order to rename body of water amid US trade spat with Canada

Apple has renamed Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for US users of its Maps app, after an executive order from Donald Trump to change the name of the Great Lake amid his trade spat with Canada.

The Apple Maps app now displays the controversial new name for the lake, which sits between New York state and the Canadian province of Ontario, for users in the US. Apple users outside the country will still see the Lake Ontario name.

Apple had been reportedly mulling whether to submit to Trump’s new order after receiving a personal request from the president for the tech company to change the lake’s name.

Trump welcomed the news, declaring in a Truth Social post that the adoption of “Lake America” by Google Maps and Apple Maps meant the name change was “complete, ratified, and binding”. However, the US cannot compel Canada – or any other country – to also change the name.

The US president officially unveiled the name swap last week. He did not mention his escalating trade feud with the US’s northern neighbors in the order, but the timing suggested a retaliatory move after Canadian officials denounced Trump’s new sweeping tariffs and promised to instate tariffs of their own.

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, rejected the attempt to rename the body of water, saying in a post on social media that the lake’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

Late last month, trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed, with the US subsequently imposing a 50% tariff on several Canadian imports. Trump additionally threatened another round of 50% duties on Canadian steel, trucks, cars and auto parts to take effect in the new year. Carney retaliated with 25-50% tariffs on hundreds of US goods.

Rather than mention any of this, Trump instead said in the order that the purpose of the renaming is to honor “the policy of my Administration to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements”.

Earlier this week, Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, said in an interview with Fox Business that “the president has reached out to Apple directly” and predicted with confidence that US users would “be seeing that change coming up soon”.

Apple’s competitor, Google, already made the change over the weekend, with Google Maps now showing the Lake America branding. Google cited Trump’s order and its practice of using names assigned by the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).

In a blogpost issued on Saturday, Google said US users would see the Lake America name while users in Canada will see Lake Ontario, and “those outside of the US and Canada will see both names.”

The digital name change is unsurprising considering Google Maps was an early adopter of the Gulf of America moniker and still currently displays the title, despite the renaming hardly being a success outside US government lingo.

On Tuesday, it was reported that MapQuest, the pioneering online mapping app, reached the No 1 spot on Apple’s App Store after openly rejecting Trump’s request to rename the lake. The app simply posted a screenshot of Lake Ontario on social media last Thursday along with the caption: “We’re not changing it.”

The act of defiance was enough to catapult the app into becoming the most in-demand navigation tool in the US.

fullText:
Relocation coincides with proposed laws that opponents say would entrench power of US tech billionaires in country

Dozens of protesters converged on Peter Thiel’s mansion in Buenos Aires this week after a congressional session raised questions about the billionaire’s presence in the country.

In white masks, they held signs saying “Peter Thief” and “No to the Peter Thiel law” in front of the wrought-iron gates of the $12m (£8.9m) residence, which Thiel bought in April as he moved his family to Argentina.

There is broad unease at the tech magnate’s presence in the country. His move has been characterised as part of a plan to hedge against world war three: Argentina, agriculturally rich and deep in the southern hemisphere, might just be the ideal place for a tech billionaire to wait out the apocalypse.

But recent developments in the country suggest Thiel could have more pragmatic considerations.

Last week, Argentina’s chamber of deputies held a six-hour debate on a set of sweeping regulatory changes put forward by Javier Milei’s rightwing government shortly after Thiel moved to Buenos Aires. They invited Thiel, Milei and an official linked to Argentina’s intelligence services to answer questions.

“None of them answered, and none of them came to the meeting,” said Juan Marino, a member of the chamber of deputies and the leader of the Piquetero party.

Marino said the new laws amounted to a “technofascist legislative package” aimed at entrenching the power of US tech billionaires in the country. Thiel has not publicly advocated for them, but Marino and others have said that their timing was suggestive.

The meeting in the chamber of deputies came after Argentinian deputies from several parties made public requests to the government for information about Thiel, his meetings and his businesses. None have been answered.

One of the laws, the “super RIGI”, would put in place an investment regime offering foreign companies a minimal tax rate and a 30-year guarantee against regulatory change. It specifically names AI datacentres among investments it hopes to attract.

Another, which failed, aimed to eliminate most of the restrictions around foreigners buying land in Argentina. A final decree would require some civilian government departments to share vast amounts of personal data on Argentinian citizens with the state intelligence services.

There is no evidence that Thiel has advocated for these laws directly. But in the months after he moved to Buenos Aires, he held closed-door meetings with Milei and key presidential advisers. It is uncommon for a foreign investor to have this degree of access.

In the regulatory package, Marino and others see the footprint of Thiel’s larger techno-libertarian interests.

The decree that gives vast amounts of Argentinians’ personal data to state intelligence services comes as Argentinian deputies have asked increasingly pointed questions about whether Palantir, the company Thiel co-founded, has undisclosed contracts with the state, which have gone unanswered.

The land law, said Marino, could have paved the way for semi-autonomous “startup cities” – such as the controversial Próspera development in Honduras – that Thiel has advocated as a way for libertarians to carve out zones outside state control.

“Argentina is kind of a laboratory,” said Cecilia Nicolini, who represents Argentina at the Mercosur regional parliament. US tech billionaires, she said, “are using Argentina as a laboratory, because they have a person in power, Milei, who is even more crazy than they are”.

Over the summer Milei wrote an article in the Financial Times advocating the creation of “non-human corporations” – “entities operated by AI agents or robots”.

It parallels a vision put forward by OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, who predicted in 2024 that the world could soon be run by AI-owned companies. It also raises dark, thorny questions about the legal liabilities of those entities.

Nicolini said: “It’s not just that [Thiel] chose Argentina in terms of, it’s a secure place to live in a world that is facing a number of wars, etcetera.

“But really, behind it, I think there is a clear plan. And it is related to reforms that Milei is trying to pass, with some success in some cases, and in others, backlash.”

Thiel was approached for comment.

title: 'Somatics' Became the Solution to Modern Life
description: The word isn’t new—but lately, it’s everywhere.
fullText:
When clients go to Sybil Ottenstein for therapy, they tend to arrive with answers. Many of them have seen shrinks before. They can tell her which events from their past were formative, and point to the ripple effects in their current life. They’re like detectives, she told me, with all the dots connected on their corkboard of evidence. Intellectually, they’ve cracked the case. The problem is that they don’t feel any better.

That’s why they’re seeking something different from Ottenstein: somatic psychotherapy. Traditional talk therapy could be seen as a top-down approach. You identify problems in your thinking, your habits, or your life, and hope that by working through them, you can resolve physical manifestations of emotional issues—the chest palpitations of anxiety, the stomachache of stress. Somatic therapy, by contrast, works from the bottom up. Ottenstein typically starts her sessions by asking clients to slow down and pay attention to corporeal sensations: “What does it feel like in your chest? In your throat?” As they talk, she encourages them to stay in their body, to let themselves feel whatever is coming up. People cry. They yawn. They scream. They stretch. They dance.

The word somatic, according to Merriam-Webster, merely means “of, relating to, or affecting the body.” But recently, it’s been popping up everywhere, appended to a variety of practices that involve tuning in to physical symptoms in order to ameliorate psychological ones. Somatic therapists like Ottenstein have noticed a significant bump in interest; one of the major somatic-therapy training programs reported that its applicants more than doubled from 2020 to 2023. Other practitioners offer somatic dance, somatic yoga, somatic workouts. (The terms seem a touch redundant.)

Read: How did healing ourselves get so exhausting?

On Instagram, hundreds of thousands of posts appear with the hashtag #somatic. A “somatic exercise” trainer who goes by the “Workout Witch” (nearly 2 million followers) teaches small, repetitive movements meant to discharge negative feelings—curl your head down for “sorrow/despair,” pull your right ear for “overwhelm”—and promises that “trauma can be released from your hips.” All over my feed, fit young women are humming, hitting their sternum, pinching their nose bridge, and bouncing their knees all the way to inner peace.

Read: These Millennials can’t get out of their head

Much of the time, as with many other wellness ventures, someone stands to make money. At one somatic-workout class I attended, where a staffer told me that the goal was to “move stagnant energy out,” the lobby featured a gift-shop corner with jewelry, T-shirts, and $65 “body gloss” from a brand called Oui the People. But clearly, plenty of Americans are willing to pay for the promise of a psychic cleanse. Practitioners refer to “stuck energy,” to “trapped emotions,” to “resetting” a nervous system caught in fight-or-flight mode. “We have all these ways of just storing that gunk inside,” Ottenstein told me. I pictured, uncomfortably, a thick, black goo running through my veins.

Somatics—the whole roomy umbrella of practices—might seem like an odd fit for the information age, when people are more accustomed to finding answers on the internet than within themselves. But that could be precisely the draw for thinkers and analyzers who are tired of ruminating in anxious circles, who spend their days in front of a laptop and nights scrolling an iPhone. For millennia, people have yearned to break out of the confines of their bodies; they’ve searched—through religion, spirituality, drugs—for transcendence. Now, for some, the existential quest is inverted: Instead of seeking to escape their prison of flesh and bones, they want to reinhabit it.

The origin of somatics is difficult to pinpoint, though it’s certainly not recent. Some credit Wilhelm Reich, a student of Freud’s, who theorized in the early 1900s that patients held tension in their bodies—“muscular armor”—as a subconscious defense against trauma, leading to aches, pains, and inflammation. But it wasn’t until the 1970s that the field began to formalize, developed in part by the American philosophy professor Thomas Hanna, who defined somatics as the study of “the body as perceived from within.” That same decade, a UC Berkeley biophysics doctoral student, Peter Levine, developed “somatic experiencing”: a therapeutic method based on the idea that people, like other animals, react to trauma with a flight, fight, or freeze response, powered by a burst of adrenaline. After the source of danger is gone, Levine argued, they have pent-up “survival energy” to unleash: They need to physically shake it off. He pointed to videos of impalas, quaking and buckling after surviving a cheetah attack. When humans go through something upsetting, Ottenstein told me, “we go to work the next day.”

This idea—that trauma is held in the body, and thus must be physically remedied—was once fairly niche. In recent years, though, it has been jolted into prominence. The psychiatrist Bessel van der Kolk’s book The Body Keeps the Score, which argues for somatic treatments of PTSD, was first released in 2014 and was not an immediate hit. In 2021, it reached the No. 1 spot on the New York Times best-seller list for paperback nonfiction. And although it has been accused of resting on shaky science, it has continued to dominate the charts for years.

Van der Kolk wrote about violent assaults, wartime atrocities, severe childhood abuse—circumstances that many readers hadn’t directly experienced. Yet The Body Keeps the Score seemed to resonate anyway. When it gained momentum, lots of Americans had spent the previous year safe in their homes, baking bread and taking Zoom calls. (“When people say the pandemic has been a collective trauma,” van der Kolk told The Atlantic that year, “I say, absolutely not.”) Most had also, however, been detached from the rich sensory experience of interacting with the external world. Now here was a book about people who’d felt estranged from their own body—and then, through simple movement, play, and touch, found their way back to their surroundings, and to themselves.

Read: The self-help that no one needs right now

In the years since, most people have emerged from pandemic isolation. Yet the share of Americans who say they frequently experience stress, which has been rising for decades, has continued its upward trend. Talk therapy remains popular, but it’s not always affordable or accessible—and much of the time, it doesn’t take physical symptoms into account. Meanwhile, many medical doctors don’t consider psychological causes of physical ailments. Stress in particular is “like this mythical creature,” Aditi Nerurkar, a physician at Harvard Medical School, told me. “And we don’t have a lot of time. We have to focus on your hemoglobin. Did you get a mammogram? Did you get a pap smear? What is your cholesterol?”

No wonder, then, that somatics is a flourishing industry. Many Americans already distrust medical institutions; maybe they want to bypass the dismissive doctor, or the therapist who wants to rehash every daddy issue but can’t seem to fix anything. So they turn to this strange constellation of New Age–y courses, TikTok sages, and licensed counselors. Some offerings target people with capital-T Trauma; others claim to be for just about anyone. Many present themselves as alternatives to more traditional paths to mental well-being. The question is whether they can really help the frazzled masses.

Somatics does get a lot of things right. Plenty of bodily sensations are, at root, psychological. Some communication does need to happen between the brain and the rest of the body. That’s how you know to respond to danger: The amygdala triggers the nervous system to increase your heart rate, deliver more blood to muscles, and release a flood of adrenaline. When I spoke with Nerurkar, she rattled off an incomplete list of physical symptoms that might result from stress: headaches, dizziness, nausea, vision changes. When she was in residency training, she said, she experienced what felt like a “stampede of wild horses” across her chest and was convinced that she had a heart problem—until her doctors, having conducted a battery of tests, recommended that she seriously consider chilling out.

And many components of somatic practice have evidence to back them up. Interoception, or awareness of one’s own physical signals, really can be important for well-being—perhaps because it increases people’s sense of attunement with their body, connection with the present moment, or agency over otherwise vague and inscrutable sensations. Mindfulness meditation, which involves interoception, has been shown to decrease stress and anxiety and even reduce physical pain. Yoga and breathing exercises can decrease amygdala activation and lead to better concentration, memory, and executive function.

But the somatics packaging of these techniques is alluring partly because of the emotional liberation it promises. Somaticists tend to describe a clear path: identify a physical signal, connect it to its psychic cause, then let it go. If the nervous system overactivates, surely you can just reset it. If the body holds trauma, surely the body can relinquish it.

These were always just metaphors, though, and imperfect ones. The amygdala doesn’t have a reboot button. There is no viscous gunk of emotional pain to flush out. The Body Keeps the Score has been somewhat debunked; critics have argued that van der Kolk incorrectly described certain studies, and that he seems to have made up others entirely. (Responding to the writer Emi Nietfeld’s critique in Mother Jones, van der Kolk said that at times he drew on unpublished data.) Trauma experts have pushed back on his wholesale condemnation of talk therapy, which can be, according to a mountain of evidence, very helpful for treating PTSD. There’s also something ironic in how certain somaticists—ostensibly advocates for the mind-body connection—talk as if the two are separated by a nearly unbridgeable gap: the physical burden of trauma unreachable through thinking or conversation, and perhaps not even accessible to conscious awareness.

Read: Why we’re still talking about the ‘trauma plot’

So somatics isn’t a miracle cure. And it’s probably right to be skeptical of influencers who seek to collect on people’s need to feel at home in their body. But that doesn’t mean somatics can’t be helpful. Much of it, after all, turns out to be pretty straightforward. Movement is good, generally. Breathing is good. Stepping away from your screen—stretching your limbs, remembering you are real and tangible and mortal—is good.

When I signed up for that somatic-exercise class, I expected that I might leave rolling my eyes, but I secretly hoped I’d walk out lighter, more alive and connected to myself and the world. What I found was something in between. The actual workout couldn’t have been more basic: It consisted largely of squats, jumping jacks, crunches, some yoga—downward dog, child’s pose. Occasionally the instructor would remind us to check in with our bodies: “What are you being invited into? And I don’t mean the burpee.” Or: “Let the chin enter the conversation.” Otherwise it hardly seemed uniquely somatic, or uniquely anything.

Then again, I had the post-workout endorphin glow. I’d left my apartment and shut my phone in a locker. An hour later, I exited the studio somewhat baffled. But walking out onto a busy Manhattan street, I felt a little more conscious of the sun on my cheek, the solidness of the ground pushing against my feet. This was silly, I thought. And also: Maybe I’ll come back.

title: The Fight for Serious AI Regulation Just Won a Big Victory in Massachusetts
description: John...
fullText:
After his primary win, Ed Markey says he’s ready to take on “the criminal enterprises” of Big Tech.

Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey won a major primary election victory on Tuesday, claiming another win for the left in this summer’s struggle for the soul of the Democratic Party. “Tonight is a testament to the power of the progressive movement,” Markey declared to a cheering crowd in which his young supporters celebrated a 65–35 triumph over his primary rival, US Representative Seth Moulton.

It was also, the senator explained, a victory in the fight against what he described as “the criminal enterprises of Big Oil and Big Tech.” A longtime foe of corporate greed and monopoly, Markey made stymieing the plans of AI oligarchs a crucial part of his campaign. With progressive-populist enthusiasm, he promised to “tax the rich, block the bombs, and stop data centers from polluting our communities.”

This is not a new fight for Markey. As the senator noted earlier this year, he’s been “working for more than a decade to propose commonsense policies to take back unchecked power from Big Tech and put it into the hands of the American people.”

But what made Markey’s victory notable was that, in the last days of the primary campaign, he faced and overcame a cynical attack from Moulton, who attempted to dumb down the AI debate in a way that he thought would turn voters against the incumbent.

Moulton’s primary challenge to Markey was always tough to fathom. A middle-aged congressman with limitless ambition but finite political skills—as evidenced by his failed bid for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination—Moulton tried to make the fight a generational struggle between a 47-year-old rival and an 80-year-old incumbent. The message never got traction because Markey campaigned relentlessly as an energetic progressive legislator with a record of standing on the right side of history.

Yet Moulton’s desperation to make the race a referendum on youth-versus-age made the last days before Tuesday’s primary contest an instructive measure of the emerging discourse over AI regulation.

When the two candidates clashed in a pre-primary debate last month, Markey gave an uninspired answer to a silly question about whether he uses AI tools on his electronic devices. He basically said he used the apps that were on his iPhone and iPad and left it at that.

Moulton, who talked during the campaign about “winning the AI race while making sure our kids, our economy, and our communities are protected,” seized on what he thought was an opening to catch up with an incumbent who was opening a wide lead in the polls. “Not understanding the basics of AI—the most important technology of our lifetime—should be disqualifying for a U.S. Senator,” he announced on social media. “This is why we need a new generation of leadership. The future is now.”

Then he pinned the message to the top of his X feed. Then he made a campaign ad. Then the challenger said, “Americans are genuinely concerned about AI. Octogenarians in the Senate are not helping.”

The campaigns also traded charges about Moulton’s investment in defense contractors, including “an AI firm that partners with the U.S. Army,” and how Markey had received the support of a nonprofit backed by Anthropic, a firm that has supported AI regulation

Amid all this bluster, Markey kept his cool, while Moulton revealed his naïveté regarding the debate over AI.

That debate is about a lot more than ruminations on the relative merits of ChatGPT and Claude. It is a fight over who will set the rules for our future.

The mounting pressure to meet the demands of the AI billionaires—to whom Donald Trump pays so much deference—raises fundamental questions about corporate power, privacy, the future of work, and a host of other issues. These are issues that Markey—long a leading Senate advocate for worker rights and consumer protection—has been focused on for years. And they are issues on which he has displayed far more insight and agility than most members of Congress.

Obituary

 /

 Nick Murray

Markey’s detailed “AI Accountability Agenda: Taking Power Back From Big Tech” program pulls together groundbreaking legislative proposals to regulate data centers and to address the broader impacts of AI—including the No Robot Bosses Act, which “would prohibit an employer from primarily relying on automated systems for work-related decisions such as hiring, firing, or promotion. The legislation would also require employers to disclose to their employees their use of an automated decision system; conduct detailed evaluations of an automated system’s impact on workers before using the system; and provide an employee with the option to appeal to a human any decision involving an automated system.”

The senator has also proposed and supported legislation to create a human override option for AI decisions that might limit access to healthcare, infringe on privacy rights, or endanger children, and to prevent AI-powered algorithms from amplifying the biases and discrimination that is already embedded in society.

Markey’s even got a plan to prevent the concentration of wealth and power in the hands of AI oligarchs. His Equal Tax Act “would tax investment income at the same rate as ordinary labor income for individuals making more than $1 million. The bill would limit preferential tax rates for long-term capital gains and dividends, end the stepped-up basis loophole, restrict the use of like-kind exchanges by the ultra-wealthy, and limit the passthrough deduction for high-income individuals. By closing loopholes that reward wealth over work, the Equal Tax Act would ensure that the people who profit most from the AI boom pay their fair share.”

Voters recognize that the fight over AI cannot be reduced to election-eve jibes over which candidate might more ably manipulate apps on a phone. It is an existential struggle over questions of whether those with wealth and power will roll over workers, consumers, and civil rights. “Americans,” Markey has explained, “deserve policymakers who are paying attention to their lives, not Big Tech’s bottom line.” By an overwhelming margin, Massachusetts voters gave Ed Markey a mandate to continue serving as that sort of policymaker.
