title: Iran warns US against Israeli attack on south Lebanon ridge held by Hezbollah, sources say
description: Iran has warned the United States that it would respond forcefully to an Israeli offensive on a mountainous ridge in southern Lebanon where Iranian military
fullText:
BEIRUT, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Iran has warned the United States that it would respond forcefully to an Israeli offensive on a mountainous ridge in southern Lebanon where Iranian military personnel are holed up alongside Hezbollah fighters, three officials briefed on the message told Reuters.

The message, delivered last month, highlights Iran's continued direct involvement in ‌the ground fighting in southern Lebanon and its readiness to retaliate against Israeli attacks there as the regional war enters its seventh month.

Hezbollah is believed to have built an ‌underground command center and weapons stores within the Ali al-Taher ridge, which has a commanding view of southeastern Lebanon, according to Lebanese security sources, and has become one of the most contested pieces of ground in the Israel-Hezbollah war.

Hezbollah has said ​in public statements that it controls the hill and will confront any Israeli advances. Its officials have referred to a "facility" there, but have declined to provide details.

The Israeli military has occupied swathes of territory to Ali al-Taher's south and has identified the ridge as one of its "primary operational focuses" in public statements.

In its message to Washington, Tehran threatened that any full-fledged Israeli offensive on the ridge would be met with a large-scale Iranian attack, said the three officials in the region, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.

Hezbollah declined to comment on whether Iranian forces were present in Ali al-Taher. In response to Reuters questions about the ‌message, or whether the U.S. had put pressure on Israel not ⁠to attack Ali al-Taher, a White House official said, "this is not accurate." There was no immediate comment from Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, the U.S. Defense Department, or Oman's foreign ministry. The Israeli military declined to comment.

IRGC FORCES HOLED UP, OFFICIALS SAY

Two of the officials said the message was delivered via Oman, which has ⁠played a mediating role. Those two regional officials, briefed by Tehran, said over a dozen members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, including at least two senior officers, were with Hezbollah fighters.

The third source, a foreign official with direct knowledge of the message, said it was delivered around mid-August and that as a result of U.S. pressure, Israel had put off storming Ali al-Taher.

Contacted by Reuters, Hezbollah's media office neither confirmed nor denied Iran's message ​but ​said it was a "natural conclusion" that such a warning would have been sent about the ridge.

"Iran considers any ​Israeli move on the ground in southern Lebanon, especially territorial expansion, a major ‌violation of the Islamabad Agreement," Hezbollah's media office said, referring to the June U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding that included a Lebanon ceasefire.

Iran fired missiles towards Israel in early June in retaliation for attacks on Hezbollah on the Lebanese capital's outskirts.

ISRAEL SEEKS TO BESIEGE HEZBOLLAH FIGHTERS

Despite a ceasefire announced in June, the Israeli military has said Hezbollah is still operating around the ridge and twice over the last week launched explosive drones towards Israeli troops near the ridge.

In July, it said it had launched an air strike on a Hezbollah fighter near an access shaft to the underground site at Ali al-Taher and vowed not to allow Hezbollah to operate in the area or pose a threat to Israeli soldiers.

An Israeli military official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told Reuters in June that Hezbollah fighters ‌were stuck underground without food or water. Israeli newspaper Maariv, citing a military source, said on Thursday that ​the Israeli military assessed there were no IRGC forces in Ali al-Taher and that some Hezbollah fighters had died without ​food and water.

The third official said Israel's military was trying to smoke out Hezbollah and IRGC ​personnel by besieging them, shooting down attempted drone deliveries of food and water to the ridge.

"What we have seen over the past month is Israeli pressure ‌to besiege Ali al-Taher in order to impose a reality within this facility ​that renders it uninhabitable. This approach, and the ​absence of a large-scale attack, means that it is possible a message was conveyed through several countries -- this is a natural conclusion," Hezbollah's media office told Reuters.

HEZBOLLAH THREATENS RETALIATION

A Lebanese source briefed by Hezbollah said the group's fighters can still access their positions through the ridge's northern side.

Despite Iran's warning, the Lebanese source and a senior Lebanese security official said an Israeli military operation to capture the ridge was still possible in the ​coming weeks.

Hezbollah said any large-scale attack on Ali al-Taher would mean a return to full-blown war, and could see missiles landing on northern Israeli communities.

title: Immigrant rights group seeks to block use of federal databases it says could purge legal voters
description: An immigrant rights group sued the Trump administration Wednesday to block the U.S. Department of Homeland Security from using federal databases that it alleged are being used to target naturalized ci...
fullText:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — An immigrant rights group sued the Trump administration Wednesday to block the U.S. Department of Homeland Security from using federal databases that it alleged are being used to target naturalized citizens who are eligible to vote.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Washington on behalf of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, alleges that DHS and the U.S. Justice Department are interfering with fair elections by using inaccurate federal databases in an attempt to buttress allegations of voter fraud.

The federal government is engaging in an "attack on the freedom to vote," Angelica Salas, the coalition's executive director, said at a downtown Los Angeles news conference. "This is voter intimidation."

The lawsuit — filed on behalf of the coalition by the UCLA Voting Rights Project — becomes part of a swirl of legal moves that states, including California, have taken to fend off federal actions that threaten to create confusion during the midterms.

"It's not an accident the federal government is trying to interfere with the right to vote. ... They believe they can intimidate naturalized U.S. citizens," said Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for California governor who is acting as a senior adviser to the voting project.

The lawsuit alleges that the administration might be comparing voter rolls with undisclosed government databases. Those systems can include outdated information and be riddled with errors, it said, and could produce inaccurate results that disproportionately affect naturalized voters.

"Comparing government databases to try and arrive at a list of noncitizen registrants has been shown to result in erroneous data," the lawsuit said. "Congress has never authorized such activities and in fact has ... prohibited invasion of voter privacy through government data matches in this way."

The Trump administration has been targeting noncitizen voting to allege it could be a source of significant fraud during the midterm elections, even though actual voting by people who are not citizens is rare. He is pushing for the U.S. Postal Service to send mail ballots only to voters verified as U.S. citizens, and his Justice Department has sued to force the release of detailed voter data in 30 states and the District of Columbia, though it has not yet succeeded in those cases.

Asked to respond to the lawsuit, a DHS spokesperson said in an email: "The department accessed publicly available data from states' voter rolls and cross referenced them with known illegal aliens in our systems. It's not rocket science; it's an easy step to secure our elections."

"DHS is laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens," the statement added.

In June, a federal judge ruled that a recently revamped version of a federal tool can no longer be used, which critics had referred to as an unlawful centralized federal database of voter information.

U.S. District Court Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan sided with advocacy groups that argued the recent upgrades to the program, called Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, aggregated Americans' sensitive personal data in a way that could result in voters being wrongly purged from voter rolls.

The lawsuit said it isn't clear if the administration used that system to generate projections about noncitizens on voting rolls in the states or if other unknown datasets were involved.

Specifically, the lawsuit by the immigrant rights group asks the court to stop the administration from pursuing a review of California's voter list and to rescind the letter sent to the state requesting voter information. It also asks the court to declare the administration's actions unconstitutional.

Trump's Department of Homeland Security is claiming without providing evidence that 250,000 noncitizens might be on the rolls in just four states, including 190,832 in California.

California's secretary of state, Democrat Shirley Weber, said in response, "I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official."

According to the lawsuit, federal officials have not disclosed evidence supporting those figures.

title: White House defends Trump’s beef import plan after report on billionaire’s influence
description: The White House defended President Trump’s decision to temporarily suspend higher tariffs on ground beef imports amid a report that a Brazilian billionaire influenced the decision. “President Trump’s ...
fullText:
The White House defended President Trump's decision to temporarily suspend higher tariffs on ground beef imports amid a report that a Brazilian billionaire influenced the decision.

"President Trump's action to address a short-term supply crunch in the beef market was the result of a long policy planning and coordination process involving domestic stakeholders; this action was not done as the result of any one conversation," a White House official told NewsNation, The Hill's sister network.

"At the same time, the Trump Administration continues to work with American farmers and ranchers to grow America's cattle herd, which is currently at a multi-decade low," the official continued.

Trump in a social media post Friday announced the suspension on ground beef tariffs, saying it would be for 90 days and would allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported at a 25 percent discount below market price.

The president wrote that the deal — which has received criticism from GOP lawmakers — was intended to "substantially lower the price of ground beef for working American families" and "reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again."

When asked at Joint Base Andrews which countries were involved in the deal, Trump said, "There are a few countries, but they're going to be sending in the highest quality beef, and it's something that we need."

The day before the announcement, Trump reportedly met with Joesley Batista — who shares control of JBS, the world's largest meatpacker — in the Oval Office, according to a Monday report from The Wall Street Journal.

The Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that during this meeting, Batista lobbied Trump to drop the 26 percent import tax as a solution to the rising cost of the diet staple.

The report noted that Pilgrim's Pride, the U.S.'s second-largest chicken processor and controlled by JBS, contributed $5 million to Trump's inauguration, making it the biggest donor.

Batista and his brother Wesley Batista were previously fined in 2020 by the Justice Department over charges that they violated the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act by using funds obtained through a bribery scheme to expand its U.S. operations. They agreed to pay a $256 million fine.

The Batistas also admitted at the time to spending roughly $150 million to bribe more than 1,800 Brazilian government officials to secure $1.3 billion in loans from the Brazilian Development Bank and federal pension funds.

title: Netherlands moves billions in gold to London in 'crisis preparedness' move
description: The Dutch central bank removes some of its gold reserves from the US and Canada, saying it is because of "increasing geopolitical unrest".
fullText:
The Dutch central bank (DNB) has confirmed that billions of dollars in gold has been taken out of north America and relocated to London, citing "increasing geopolitical unrest".

DNB said on Wednesday that 86 tonnes of gold had been removed from the US and Canada in a complex operation that took several months. It is now being held by the Bank of England, where the precious metal can be traded more easily "in a crisis situation".

Bank president Olaf Sleijpen said the move was "necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness".

The decision comes amid an ongoing trade dispute between the US and Canada, with both countries announcing fresh tariffs on each other after failed trade talks.

DNB said the transfer, which took place between March and August, saw 27 tonnes of gold bars moved from New York and Ottawa to Zeist in the Netherlands.

A similar quantity and quality was then moved to London, with no need to melt the bars down.

Exactly how so much gold was transported across the Atlantic Ocean has not been revealed.

The rest of the transfer was carried out by selling the gold in New York, and repurchasing it in London, the bank said.

"Combining the processes of buying and selling and physical transport has allowed DNB to spread the risks associated with such a complex physical gold relocation," the statement said.

DNB did not confirm what it was referring to with its mention of "geopolitical unrest" but the US economy remains in an uncertain position due to the country's ongoing war with Iran, which has impacted global trade.

Canada, meanwhile, has been hit hard by US tariffs on its key sectors of steel, aluminium, lumber and automobiles as well as an additional 50% levy on about C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) of Canadian goods announced in August.

DNB said that gold that is held with the Bank of England "is regarded as the world's most easily tradable gold," and therefore more readily available in a crisis than if it was still in the US or Canada.

Prior to Wednesday's announcement, the DNB held 31.3% of its gold in New York and 19.7% in Ottawa. This has now fallen to 18.5% in both countries.

The total Dutch gold stock was 612.4 tonnes at the end of 2025 and has been valued at €72.2 billion, DNB said.

The bank's share of gold in London has increased from 18.1% to 32.1% after the move, while it still holds 30.8% of its reserves in the Netherlands.

title: Spanberger's ICE restrictions dealt major setback as judge warns other blue states
description: A federal judge blocked a key part of Gov. Abigail Spanberger's law restricting local 287(g) cooperation with ICE, and Republicans say they warned her.
fullText:
A judge paused a key part of Virginia's new restrictions on local cooperation with federal immigration authorities, handing Gov. Abigail Spanberger's administration a major legal setback as a similar fight plays out in neighboring Maryland.

George H.W. Bush-appointed Judge Robert Payne on Monday blocked a key piece of a law signed by Gov. Abigail Spanberger that heavily restricts interagency cooperation and would have required local sheriffs to modify or dissolve their individual policies, known as 287(g) agreements, by a Tuesday deadline.

Payne ruled the federal government is likely to prevail on several claims in its lawsuit against Virginia, finding "the Virginia 287(g) Law violates the Contracts Clause [of the] U.S. Constitution because it is a 'substantial impairment' of the existing contracts between the federal government and Virginia localities."

Payne did not strike down the law but paused its implementation as the feds' case against Richmond proceeds.

First On Fox: Doj Sues Spanberger's Virginia Over Laws Kneecapping Federal Agents As Mask War Escalates

He also found that Virginia's law wrongly attempts to "regulate conduct of federal law enforcement in the enforcement of federal immigration laws."

"At this point, saying 'I told you so' seems almost pointless," Virginia House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore, R-Gate City, told Fox News Digital when responding to the news.

Legal Expert Unleashes On Spanberger's New Executive Order Targeting Ice: 'Political Theater'

Kilgore said Republicans repeatedly warned Spanberger's administration that its limits on cooperation with ICE would waste taxpayer money and run into these kinds of legal problems.

"States cannot tell the federal government how to do its job. But Democrats refused to listen," Kilgore said.

In that regard, Rep. Ben Cline, R-Va., drafted a bill at the federal level aimed directly at Spanberger's law.

Cline's 287(g) Cooperation Act would require state and local law enforcement to enter into interagency agreements with ICE as a condition of receiving federal Community-Oriented Policing (COPS) grants.

Additionally, all five of Virginia's Republican members of Congress wrote Spanberger earlier this year urging her not to undo former Gov. Glenn Youngkin's statewide directive of Richmond-Washington cooperation on the immigration enforcement front.

The major setback to Democrats' plans came as neighboring Maryland found itself in a similar legal fight, though a judge has not yet ruled in that case.

Hochul Remains Defiant After Sheriffs Sue Over Law Banning Cooperation With Ice: 'Bring It On'

Gov. Wes Moore allowed a similar bill to become law earlier this year that would prevent most cooperation between local sheriffs and ICE. Despite Maryland being one of the bluest states in the union, the majority of its counties are geographically red.

That dynamic revealed itself as 17 of its 24 sheriffs, led by Harford County's Jeffrey Gahler, Wicomico County's Mike Lewis and Frederick County's Charles Jenkins launched a lawsuit against the law.

"They want to do everything they can to handcuff law enforcement, handcuff sheriffs across the state," Jenkins said in March.

Sen. Clarence Lam, D-Elkridge, a bill sponsor, argued the measure ensures local jails won't be used as a "front door to the federal government's oftentimes deportation pipeline," according to Maryland Matters.

Lam's Community Trust Act requires a court order to provide immigration-related information and to transfer inmates based on immigration status, according to the outlet.

Moore did not sign the legislation, but it became law after he notified Senate President Bill Ferguson IV, D-Baltimore, of his decision after the bill passed 32-15.

Gahler's coalition later sued, setting up a potentially similar battle in Greenbelt federal court to the one making a splash across the Potomac.

fullText:
The Trump administration has suggested federal agencies may stop working with the Smithsonian Institution if its leadership does not change, ramping up a monthslong pressure campaign to align the world's largest museum complex with its views.

In an August 28 letter to the Smithsonian's governing body that was recently made public, administration officials said government agencies cannot "in good conscience" support the institution and may cease "loaning artifacts for exhibits, enabling procurement processes and making discretionary grants," citing a White House report that claimed the institution was promoting "extreme political activism" at the National Museum of American History in Washington, DC.

It's a sign that the Trump administration is considering more aggressive measures to exert influence on content at the Smithsonian, which has tried to maintain its independence despite unprecedented scrutiny of its programming. President Donald Trump has tasked aides with rooting out "woke" ideology and what he considers a rewriting of American history at the museums.

"Because these concerns arise from executive leadership and institutional ideology at the Smithsonian, the appropriate response must likewise address executive leadership and institutional ideology," wrote Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Vince Haley, the director of the White House's Domestic Policy Council, in the letter.

They also wrote that the administration has "recently uncovered evidence" that the Smithsonian's "institutional culture may have resulted in significant violations of Federal antidiscrimination law" without providing examples. CNN has reached out to the Smithsonian and the Interior Department for comment and more information.

While the 179-year-old institution is a unique public-private trust and does not consider itself an executive agency, the federal government supplies two-thirds of its budget. The government also frequently collaborates with the Smithsonian on museum initiatives and research projects.

In the letter, the officials asked the Smithsonian's Board of Regents to meet with them in person to discuss the White House's findings, which were released on July 4. The National Museum of American History's Director, Andrea Hartig, said at a July congressional hearing that the report "does not fairly or accurately characterize the full body of work at the museum."

"The museum does not take sides in America's political debates. We preserve and document the evidence of American life in all of its breadth, so that the public can encounter the past and draw their own conclusions," she said.

The letter comes weeks after Trump ordered the National Park Service to install temporary signage near the American history museum that warned of "inaccurate information" in the exhibits.

White House scrutiny of the Smithsonian dates back to March 2025, when Trump signed an executive order directing Vice President JD Vance to seek the appointment of public members to the Smithsonian's Board of Regents who are aligned with his priorities for the institution. Months later, the White House launched an unprecedented, sweeping review of the Smithsonian, asking for extensive documents about its museum exhibitions and operations.

Members of the board include Chief Justice John Roberts, Republican and Democratic members of Congress, and members of the public who are mostly former business executives and nonprofit board members.

Two of nine public regents' terms have expired and two other spots will open up by the beginning of October, according to a term chart on the Smithsonian website. This could give Trump a chance to try to expand his influence on the board before the November midterm elections shake up Congress. New board members are appointed via congressional joint resolutions that the president must sign into law.

CNN reported earlier this year that there is unanimity among the citizen members that the Smithsonian should remain independent and not be influenced by the administration.

Lonnie Bunch III, the institution's head since 2019, told CNN in a May interview that the institution has maintained its autonomy as it complied with the White House's request for information.

"My goal is that history is driven by scholarship, not partisanship," he said. "The Smithsonian always does its own scholarship. It's always driven by that. We have always worked with different administrations, but it's always about what our scholarship tells us."

CNN's Renee Marsh, Aleena Fayaz and Michael Williams contributed to this report.

title: With Japan tightening rules for foreign residents, some wonder if it’s time to say ‘sayonara’
description: Only 3.4% of Japan’s population is immigrants. But tougher rules and higher fees are making it even more difficult for foreigners to obtain residency.
fullText:
Zen gardens, futuristic cityscapes and a vibrant food scene, combined with a favorable exchange rate against the yen, have turned Japan into a tourist magnet that has been drawing in record numbers of visitors in recent years.

The number of people settling down for longer-term stays, including work and study, also hit an all-time high last year, likely due to the reliable safety and convenient infrastructure the world's fourth-largest economy has to offer.

But recently, a series of tightened immigration policies imposed by the government has made those who've come to call Japan their second home wonder: Is it time to say "sayonara"?

Japan has a long history of strict immigration policies and a homogeneous population. However, gripped by a spiraling demographic crisis, the country gradually opened up to foreign workers as well as seeking more international tourists.

But such efforts did not wholly succeed.

Overtourism and reports — some true, others misconceived — of foreign residents flouting local rules have recently fueled the rise of "Japan-first" politics and reshaped the trajectory of what was becoming a more open, diverse and welcoming society.

Last month, the Japanese government, led by conservative Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, said that a range of visa fees would rise in October — the latest in a series of stricter measures for foreigners.

Under the new rules, those looking to settle permanently in Japan will have to fork out 20 times more — 200,000 yen ($1,257) — to become a permanent resident.

Prices for other work and student visas will also rise.

The purpose of the spike in fees is to forge "an orderly society in which foreigners and Japanese citizens coexist," said Justice Minister Hiroshi Hiraguchi.

That left some foreign residents in Japan worrying whether it's the start of a trend of tougher policies for newcomers.

The most drastic shifts impact those who plan to stay in Japan for the longest – those applying for permanent residency, a status that grants rights to work, unlimited entries, and infinite stay.

Effective from October, applicants are required to have an income level higher than that of average Japanese households. And from next April, aspiring permanent residents need to have a projected pension fund equivalent to 30 years of payouts. They also have to speak intermediate-level Japanese.

"Considering that permanent resident is the most stable status of residence, this revision makes necessary updates to the application of independent livelihood and national interest requirements to ensure applicants do not become a public burden," said Hiraguchi during a press conference last month.

Earlier this year, the government also tightened rules for foreign business owners, raising the capital requirement of a business manager visa popular among entrepreneurs from five million yen ($31,000) to 30 million ($126,000).

The number of foreign residents recached 4.1 million last year, a record high representing about 3.4% of the Japanese population. More than 930,000 Chinese nationals live in Japan, making it the largest group, while about 70,000 Americans also reside there.

The recent changes followed reports that some foreign residents had been driving up home prices or evading payments for their public health insurance. Japan has a national healthcare system which requires every resident to pay a monthly or yearly fee in order to access discounted medical services.

Others have been accused of exploiting the relatively affordable policies to acquire residency by creating shell companies, prompting calls to plug loopholes.

A surge in tourists has also annoyed some locals, who've accused them of causing a nuisance and increasing the cost of living– problems political pundits say were sometimes wrongly attributed to foreign residents.

The anger fueled the rise of Sanseito, a minor right-wing party that rallied against immigrants in recent elections, putting pressure on the ruling Liberal Democratic Party government.

But the government's new policies have sparked concerns among foreigners who have built a life in the country.

Some business owners have complained that the new capital requirement, which surged sixfold, significantly reduced their cash flow, rendering their business unsustainable.

Many Indian and Nepali restaurants were reportedly forced to close after their owners — most of whom came from their native countries to seek business opportunities in Japan — said their visa renewals had been rejected.

One of those affected by the new regulations is a transgender teacher from the US, who asked CNN for anonymity, fearing it could jeopardize her immigration status.

Although she and her American spouse have been living in Japan for nearly 10 years and she speaks fluent Japanese, she told CNN that her plans-in-progress to become a permanent resident are now more challenging.

"Our long-term goal is always to gain permanent residency, and that in particular is outrageously expensive under the currently proposed guidelines," she said. "Obviously, it's something that we could save up for, but it's a wholly unpredicted expense."

Her gender identity also adds levels of difficulty. Currently, her passport identifies her as a man and she is married to a woman. She can't change it because Japan doesn't recognize same-sex marriage. That would eliminate the possibility of using a spousal visa in Japan, which would have provided a backup option to staying in the country should her current work visa fall through.

Tokyo-based immigration lawyer Kazuki Yuda, from Touch Immigration Law Firm, said inquiries had spiked recently as people rushed to file their applications before the new changes came in.

He said the new rules were too strict and he expected the number of people qualifying for permanent residency to drastically drop.

Takaichi's government is walking a fine line between the need to calm public anger, on which its political foes ride, while addressing the urgent need to replenish the country's workforce, at a time when its neighbors, from South Korea to Singapore, are loosening rules to attract young talent.

Japan's fertility rate — the average number of children a woman is expected to have during her lifetime — plunged to the lowest in a decade last year at 1.14, although there appeared to be a slight uptick in the first half of this year, according to official statistics.

A fertility rate of at least 2.1 is required to maintain a stable population without immigration. As a result, Japan finds itself in a precarious position, caught between a lack of locals to fill roles in the workforce and a distrust of immigrants who can provide labor.

For some, Japan was already losing its appeal as a destination for work, as the yen fell to 40-year lows against the dollar. Now worries about visa costs and the uncertainties are causing some to think twice.

"As a fresh graduate, fees like this would have been impossible for me. Even now, I'm barely scraping by," Sarah Nelkin, who came to Japan for studies more than a decade ago, wrote on X.

"Looking at the Japanese market 10 years from now, I genuinely feel from the bottom of my heart that things are heading for serious trouble," wrote Nelkin, now a media producer based in Japan.

title: Lutnick apologizes for saying no Americans have died in Iran war
description: WASHINGTON, Sept 3 (Reuters) - U.S.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 3 (Reuters) - U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick apologized on Thursday for stating ‌that no Americans had died in the ‌Iran war, acknowledging that 18 service members have been killed ​and he was thinking about Venezuela when he made the mistaken statement.

"I misspoke. Eighteen members of our military have died, and to those families my ‌heart breaks and ⁠I am so very sorry for their loss. I was thinking about the ⁠Venezuelan military operation where no service members died," Lutnick said in a post on X.

Lutnick made the comments ​during an ​interview with CNBC ​on Wednesday in which ‌Venezuela did not come up.

"I think the way the president is playing Iran... There haven't been American deaths. It's really just an economic choke-out, which the administration is now executing more broadly, ‌and I think it'll be ​very effective," Lutnick told CNBC.

Moments ​before Lutnick's apology, ​Trump defended the commerce secretary on ‌Truth Social.

"Sec. Lutnick had Venezuela ​on his ​mind when he said nobody was killed. 18 people were killed in Iran!" Trump wrote.

To ​date, the U.S. ‌has reported 18 military personnel killed and ​more than 750 wounded.

title: NJ mom fatally stabbed in Times Square during first week back at Bank of America after maternity leave
description: Erin Piacenti, a 32-year-old Bank of America executive and Fordham Law graduate, was in her first week back from maternity leave when the attack took place.
fullText:
A Bank of America executive who had recently returned to work after maternity leave was fatally stabbed Monday in New York City's Times Square, where a knife-wielding woman also wounded another person before police fatally shot the suspect.

The victim was identified as Erin Piacenti, 32, of Chester, New Jersey. Piacenti was in her first week back at Bank of America after spending five months caring for her newborn daughter, The New York Times reported.

Four days before her death, Piacenti shared a photo on social media of herself with the baby and her husband, Frank Piacenti. She also posted about the child's recent baptism and the family's travels while she was on leave.

Teen Shot In Times Square As Knicks Championship Celebrations Turn Chaotic

The NYPD said Piacenti was stabbed near West 42nd Street and Seventh Avenue before being taken to Bellevue Hospital, where she was pronounced dead.

A 68-year-old man was also stabbed in the abdomen and taken to Bellevue, where he was listed in stable condition.

Multiple People Stabbed Near Penn Station, Leaving One Seriously Injured As Investigation Continues

Police said the attack began near West 41st Street when Pamela Cisneros, 49, of Queens, approached the man while armed with two large knives. He had just exited a subway station and was waiting to cross the street with his wife.

A witness told investigators that Cisneros pulled the knives from a red Target bag before attacking the man.

Witnesses Recount 'Scary' Nyc Stabbing After Suspect Allegedly Yelled 'Allahu Akbar' During Attacks

Cisneros then moved north on Seventh Avenue and stabbed Piacenti. NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the two attacks occurred about 20 seconds apart.

Officers later confronted Cisneros while she was still holding both knives. Police recovered the weapons at the scene.

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

Cisneros refused repeated commands to drop the weapons and engaged officers in a standoff that lasted about four minutes, Tisch said. When she advanced toward officers while waving the knives, police deployed Tasers, but they failed to stop her. Two officers then fired their weapons.

"Our officers were confronted with a rapidly evolving threat, with countless innocent people around them," Tisch said.

Cisneros was taken to Bellevue, where she was pronounced dead.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

Tisch described the attack as random and unprovoked. Cisneros had documented mental health-related encounters with the NYPD in 2018 and 2019 but no prior arrest record with the department. Police said there was no indication the attack was related to terrorism.

Bank of America confirmed Piacenti's death in an emailed statement to Reuters.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"We are shocked and deeply saddened by the tragic loss of our colleague," the bank said. "She was a valued teammate who will be greatly missed."

Piacenti earned a law degree from Fordham University School of Law in 2021 alongside her husband, the school told The Associated Press. Fordham Law said it was heartbroken by the death of its former student.

The NYPD's Force Investigation Division is reviewing the police shooting. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said body-worn camera footage from the encounter will be released.

title: Trump falsely claims prices are falling rapidly. Some Republican ads acknowledge reality
description: President Donald Trump has a triumphant message on inflation. Some of his party’s television ads sound very different.
fullText:
President Donald Trump has a triumphant message on inflation. Some of his party's television ads sound very different.

Even as consumer prices continue rising, Trump continues to falsely claim that they are falling – and even that they are down since he returned to office, though they are actually up 4.3% over that period. In the past two weeks alone, Trump has claimed that "I've largely taken care of inflation," that "the prices are all coming down," that "the prices are coming down very rapidly," and that prices have already fallen "very, very, very substantially."

Fact-checkers have challenged such claims for months, but you don't have to take it from us. Some Republican midterm candidates have been running commercials that acknowledge reality – implicitly rejecting the narrative of their party's chief spokesman on one of the year's most important issues.

"On our farm here in Belle Plaine, we see it every day: gas, groceries, everything's expensive. Iowa families are hurting," Zach Lahn, the Republican candidate for governor of Iowa, says in one recent ad, going on to claim his Democratic opponent is out of touch.

"Housing costs keep rising, and it's getting harder to afford a place to live," another Iowa Republican in a competitive race, Rep. Zach Nunn, says in an ad in which he proceeds to pitch a proposal to train more skilled workers and builders.

An ad from Republican Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy features a testimonial from a woman who touts him as strong on healthcare affordability. The ad begins with the same woman delivering a broad complaint about rising costs: "When I was diagnosed with breast cancer, the last thing I needed to worry about was money. But bills are overwhelming, and groceries, rent, and gas are more expensive too."

Such messages would have fit right in four years ago. Republicans flooded the airwaves with inflation-related ads during the 2022 midterms under then-President Joe Biden, attacking him and other Democrats over price hikes that year caused in significant part by the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

As Republican candidates either vocally support Trump or tread carefully around him, this year's GOP ads on inflation don't target the president even though his own war in Iran has been the main driver of a jump in gas prices. The ads viewed by CNN, many of which were identified by the firm AdImpact upon request, tend to mention costs to establish empathy and attack Democratic opponents. They show that some Republicans are trying to go on offense on an issue in which polling suggests Democrats have erased or perhaps even reversed Republicans' prior advantage.

"Cost of living, the energy prices, the gas prices, it's really affecting those of us that live in this valley," says a man in one ad supporting Republican Rep. David Valadao of California. "In our communities, we're neighbors, not enemies, paying the same skyrocketing electric bills, taxes, and housing costs," says a narrator in an ad from Massachusetts Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Minogue.

An attack ad from a group aligned with Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas uses a narrator to deliver a series of attacks on Democratic candidate James Talarico, who is running for Texas' other US Senate seat in a competitive race against Republican Ken Paxton. Given that Trump insists prices have already fallen and are continuing to fall, it's notable that the narrator passingly asserts that prices are spiking – claiming Talarico hurt taxpayers "while your costs are skyrocketing."

And a Republican National Committee fundraising text sent out last week under the name of Vice President JD Vance made this curious pitch: "If you can't give right now, don't, (name of recipient). Groceries cost what they cost." The text didn't say anything about grocery costs having increased under the Trump-Vance administration, but it certainly didn't match the president's rosy tone on the subject.

There's a chance that Republican television ads succeed in helping to turn the cost of living into at least a neutral issue in some tight races. With memories of the Biden era still fresh, polling also suggests Democrats aren't particularly trusted on inflation.

But with midterms generally shaped by voters' views on the incumbent president, it's an uphill climb for Trump's party. Polls suggest most Americans believe Trump is to blame for high gas prices and that Trump's policies have increased the cost of living. Trump's eagerness to impose tariffs, most recently against Canada, has kept product costs in the headlines.

Some Democrats being targeted by inflation-related attacks scoff at Republicans delivering this message at the same time as Republicans control Congress and a Republican president pursues high-profile policies that have contributed to price increases.

"While Ohioans are getting crushed by rising costs, Washington Republicans are acting like they didn't send them the bill," Kylie Blitzer, campaign spokesperson for Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, said in a Monday email.

Blitzer was responding to a Republican ad that features a narrator saying, "Marcy Kaptur knows families are being crushed by rising costs," then attacks Kaptur for supposedly rejecting "real relief" by voting against Trump's tax cuts last year. Blitzer, who said Kaptur voted against the bill because it was a gift to billionaires, blasted Republicans for spending billions on the Iran war and a bailout of Argentina while "working people are paying more for nearly everything and Ohio farmers face a double whammy of skyrocketing diesel and fertilizer costs as vanity tariffs and trade wars wipe them out."

Democrats, of course, have been running lots of their own ads about the cost of living. Republicans who have sounded like Trump on the issue are particularly easy targets. On Tuesday, Roy Cooper, a Democrat running for the US Senate in North Carolina, released an ad featuring clips of his Republican opponent Michael Whatley wrongly declaring last year that "there is no inflation" and also saying "grocery prices are down, gasoline prices are down, housing prices are down, inflation is down."

Cooper, appearing incredulous, replies "unbelievable" and "seriously?"

The Cooper ad doesn't acknowledge that the Whatley comments were from 2025, when the rate of inflation was indeed lower than when Biden left office (though prices were still rising). But crying foul wouldn't help Whatley, since he would have to acknowledge that the inflation rate is now higher than when Trump was sworn back in.

CNN's David Wright contributed to this article.

title: Nigeria's economy grows at fastest pace in five years
description: President Bola Tinubu has overseen a turnaround of Africa’s third-largest economy.
fullText:
Nigeria's GDP expanded at the fastest pace in five years, boosting President Bola Tinubu's reelection pitch that his policies have stabilized a once-ailing economy. Though growth remains below official targets, Tinubu has nonetheless overseen a turnaround of the continent's third-largest economy since coming to office in 2023.

The second quarter's 4.43% growth was led by the manufacturing, agriculture and services sectors, as well as an oil sector that has benefited from higher crude prices sparked by the Iran war. Nigeria's naira currency, which weakened sharply under Tinubu following devaluations, has appreciated 12% in the twelve months to June.

Nigeria's net direct investment inflows have improved significantly under Tinubu and the oil industry is booming. However, insecurity remains a notable weak point, testing his reelection odds ahead of an election in January. Despite building security ties with the US, armed conflict and kidnappings remain rampant in much of Nigeria: The three months to June were the most violent in decades.

title: Community mourns teens found dead in Alaska hours after going missing
description: The teens' bodies were found just hours after they were reported missing Monday morning.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — The Juneau, Alaska, community is mourning the loss of 16-year-olds Leotis Phillips and Zoey Clark after they were found dead in the woods with a gun on Monday.

"I can't imagine the pain they were in to make this decision," Ariah Clark, a cousin of Zoey Clark, said at a candlelight vigil Tuesday, according to the Juneau Independent. The outlet reported that more than 150 friends, family and teachers gathered at Clark's high school for the vigil, near where the teens' bodies were found.

"The only comfort I think any of us can find at this point is that they weren't alone and they found peace in those last moments together," Clark added. "They wouldn't want any of us to continue to suffer because that was not their goal and intention."

The Juneau Police Department said the teens appeared to have died from gunshot wounds after warning in their initial announcement that they could have a firearm. The teens' bodies were found together in a wooded area in the state's capital city just hours after they were reported missing Monday morning.

The Zach Gordon Youth Center, a place where the Juneau Independent reported that Phillips spent time, posted on Facebook that it is "deeply saddened by the tragic loss of two of our precious teens," and provided resources for suicide prevention support.

"If you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts, please get help," the center wrote. "Call or text 988 and please tell an adult."

NewsNation's Josie Fischels contributed to this report.

title: Zelenskyy says foreign airlines suspend Russia flights after Ukrainian warning
description: Zelenskyy said this week that Russian airspace "will effectively be closing."
fullText:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday that the first airlines had begun suspending flights to Russian airports following his vow earlier this week to force the closure of Russian airspace through expanded drone attacks.

"We're getting word that the first airlines have started to suspend flights to Russian airports following our announcement about the drone hazard that objectively exists in Russian airspace," Zelenskyy said in a post to X.

"Ukraine has already officially informed international organizations and our partners about the real situation in Russian airspace," Zelenskyy added.

Disruption to Russian airports and flights have become routine during Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor, as Ukraine has expanded its long-range drone and missile strikes on targets deep into Russian territory.

Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow resume hours after CIA director's visit, mayor says

Ukraine scales up drone attacks in Moscow, across Russia to record highs, data shows

Each night brings temporary restrictions on flights at airports across western and southern Russia, which also often extend to Moscow's international airports.

Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia's full-scale invasion began on Feb. 24, 2022. This week, Zelenskyy said that due to "drone infested skies," Russian airspace "will effectively be closing -- the war started by Russia is closing its skies."

On Wednesday night into Thursday morning, Russia's federal air transport agency -- Rosaviatsiya -- announced temporary flight restrictions at airports in Sochi, Gelendzhik, Penza, Saratov, Yaroslavl and Nizhny Novgorod.

All four of Moscow's international airports -- Vnukovo, Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo and Zhukovsky -- were also put under flight restrictions, Rosaviatsiya said in posts to Telegram.

Russia's escalating strikes in Ukraine increasingly spilling into NATO, Romania says

Russia's Defense Ministry said that its forces downed 416 Ukrainian drones overnight into Thursday morning. The craft were shot down over 15 Russian regions, plus occupied Crimea and the Black Sea, the ministry said in a post to Telegram.

At least 116 drones were shot down en route to Moscow, the capital's Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said in posts to Telegram.

Russian authorities have dismissed Zelenskyy's warning. On Wednesday evening, Rosaviatsiya said in a statement that Ukraine's NOTAM -- a Notice to Air Missions, an official warning to air crews of flight hazards -- was "illegitimate."

"All documents published by Ukraine concerning Russian airspace have no legal force and violate the Convention on International Civil Aviation," Rosaviatsiya added. "Russian air transport, its ground infrastructure, continue to operate normally, receiving and dispatching flights, including those of foreign airlines."

'The damage is enormous': Ukraine grapples with record-breaking Russian missile strikes

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday said Zelenskyy's threat constituted "state‑sponsored terrorism." The Russian leader added that if any related air accidents occur, "We will find something to respond with."

Ukraine has significantly expanded the scale of its drone attacks into Russia in recent months, according to data published by Russia's Defense Ministry and analyzed by ABC News.

Across August, the ministry said it shot down 18,174 Ukrainian drones -- at an average rate of around 586 each day -- as well as 56 Flamingo cruise missiles.

August was the fourth month in a row that the ministry reported a new record-high total for the number of Ukrainian drones shot down. In July, the ministry said it downed 13,312 Ukrainian drones, in June 11,914 craft and in May 9,418.

title: US pressure on Iran starting to tell, as sanctions and blockade bite
description: (Widens distribution) By Parisa Hafezi and Angus McDowall DUBAI, Sept 3 (Reuters) - A U.S. campaign to throttle Iran's economy by blockading its oil exports and stopping sanctions evasion is growing
fullText:
DUBAI, Sept 3 (Reuters) - A U.S. campaign to throttle Iran's economy by blockading its oil exports and stopping sanctions evasion is growing increasingly difficult to withstand, three senior Iranian sources said.

Washington has in recent weeks sought to ratchet up the economic pressure on Tehran, in an effort to extract concessions in any future negotiation that six months ‌of conflict have so far failed to secure.

Although Iran's clerical rulers managed to bypass sanctions for decades, the latest U.S. moves have left them in a far more sensitive position, with few remaining ‌channels to secure foreign currency or buy goods, the sources said.

In particular, the effort to stop Iran accessing international financing networks in other countries it has long used to keep its economy functioning poses a real and urgent threat, the sources said.

Any sign the economic campaign may ​break a months-long deadlock in the conflict will likely cheer U.S. planners, though Iran has also warned it could respond to the pressure with military escalation, raising the stakes at a key moment.

PETROL STOCKS LOW AS CURRENCY COLLAPSES

The war has erupted back into open fighting this week, with U.S. attacks along Iran's Gulf coast prompting retaliatory Iranian strikes at U.S. bases in Arab states.

Neither side has signalled yet it is ready to make the concessions demanded by the other, leaving the war in a costly stalemate - though one that may be shifting.

While more energy is flowing to international markets through the Strait of Hormuz despite Iranian efforts to continue disrupting the seaway, the U.S. blockade of Iranian oil exports has ‌entirely cut off Tehran's main source of revenue.

Adding to Iran's problems, the economy ⁠was already deep in crisis before the conflict, with a cratering currency and spiralling inflation, while months of bombing have run up a massive bill to rebuild damaged industry and infrastructure.

Meanwhile, the country's financial squeeze is itself biting into Tehran's efforts to get around the sanctions regime, leaving less cash to pay the high premiums required to skirt ⁠sanctions illicitly, the sources said.

The rial has fallen to record lows over recent days and one senior source said Iran only has another two months' supply of gasoline, which has to be imported despite domestic oil production because of limited refining capacity.

Iran's rulers are keenly aware of the potential risks of an economic meltdown and the possibility of it reigniting the nationwide mass protests it put down in January by killing thousands of demonstrators.

"They are under very, very severe economic pressure. They're losing control ​of ​the Straits. It's really a question of if they choose to negotiate and I think they'll have to," said Ali Ansari, ​modern history professor at St Andrews University in Scotland.

The war is also entering a new ‌phase, with each side trying to influence each other's politics.

Iran hopes the threat of inflation will deter the U.S. administration before midterm elections in November, while Washington aims to push Iranians to revolt, a senior Iranian official said.

BLOCKADE AND SECONDARY SANCTIONS SQUEEZING TEHRAN

The latest U.S. measures expanded secondary sanctions that target countries doing business with Iran in a bid to stop it clearing dollar transactions needed for both oil sales and to finance crucial imports of goods and raw materials.

That effort is making Iran's existing sanctions evasion networks - front companies, unregistered tankers and smuggling - too expensive to use, the three senior sources said.

Iranian crude loadings have fallen this month to about 260,000 barrels a day, from about 1.7 million a year earlier, according to data from commodity analytics firm Kpler, with only a trickle still moving off terminals for distribution by truck, train or smaller boats over the Caspian Sea.

Tehran says it ‌still has tens of millions of barrels stored in tankers outside the blockade zone that it can sell, but the new ​sanctions mean intermediaries are stepping back or demanding more money, one of the officials said.

Total trade has fallen between 25% and 35%, ​with imports hit harder than exports, President Masoud Pezeshkian has said, one of several top officials warning ​in recent weeks about Iran's rapidly deteriorating situation.

U.S. pressure and Iran's own attacks have meanwhile disrupted one of the main conduits for Iranian trade - the United Arab Emirates, which said ‌on August 19 that all commercial exchange and financial dealings with Tehran were halted ​until further notice.

"If those channels stay closed, a supplier wants ​cash, a deal is routed through another country and a shipment arrives later and dearer," said an Iranian trader in Tehran who deals in imported goods.

The currency has collapsed in value from around 1 million rials to the dollar a year ago to over 2.2 million rials now.

The internal impact is very painful. Official figures put 12-month average inflation at 69.9% with food, beverages and tobacco prices rising at ​nearly twice that rate.

Official unemployment rose to 9.1% in the spring, while the ‌number of those in work fell by about 450,000 from a year earlier amid a wider fall in labour force participation.

Even for those still in work, the average monthly salary of around $125 ​a month comes nowhere near meeting basic household spending requirements that come to around $450 a month according to official data.

"We are getting poorer every day," said Mahnaz, a 34-year-old private-sector employee in ​Tehran who asked that her family name not be used.

(By Parisa Hafezi and Angus McDowall; Editing by Alex Richardson)

title: Organisers 'truly sorry' for cancelling festival
description: Organisers say the event in Tetbury, Gloucestershire will now take place in June 2027.
fullText:
Organisers of a music festival say they are "truly sorry" for cancelling the event which had already been postponed.

Existance Festival was due to take place at Boldridge Farm in Tetbury, Gloucestershire from 3-6 September after being postponed in June due to "compliance issues".

The festival was given the green light in August but organisers said it would not go ahead because of several issues, including the "very late" licence approval.

In a post on social media last week, the team behind Existance Festival said it would instead take place between 10-13 June 2027.

Move to support rather than punish absent pupils

'Passionate collector' selling Churchill VE Day item

'Time is running out' to save historic tall ship

Existance Festival received the licence approval on condition a traffic management plan was put in place along with adequate fire safety measures.

But the festival said the lateness of the licence approval, a fire over the summer and "issues with the supply of key infrastructure" meant the September arrangements were no longer viable.

"We have looked at a number of diﬀerent ways around these problems, but ultimately we have reached the point where proceeding would mean compromising the festival and the experience we have promised you," organisers said.

Existance Festival also apologised to ticketholders who had booked time off and arranged travel to the event.

It said those who have bought tickets would be able to use them for the new dates in June and those who are unable to attend would be entitled to a refund.

Existance - a Psytrance festival - had expected up to 2,000 people to attend the event.

The festival had previously been held near Malmesbury in Wiltshire but was forced to relocate due to noise levels - something event organisers blamed on a contractor.

title: Collins lights up internet with response to Dem challenger fathering children with relative: 'Stone cold'
description: Susan Collins used a sly rhetorical move to highlight that opponent Troy Jackson fathered two children with his second cousin during a campaign interview.
fullText:
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, had a sly way of addressing reports that Troy Jackson, her Democratic opponent, fathered two children with his second cousin.

"Well, I'm not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin," Collins told a Politico reporter when asked if Jackson's personal life would be fair game on the campaign trail. "I don't know whether people know that or not."

"But you just mentioned it," the reporter shot back.

The clip quickly spread across social media as conservatives praised Collins for her political savvy.

Top Dem Operative Brushes Off Latest Scandal Plaguing Maine Senate Candidate As 'Salacious Gossip'

Republican political operative Jesse Hunt reacted to a clip of the interview by calling Collins a "silent killer."

"A less-than-2-minute precis of how Susan Collins is as stone-cold a political combatant as the Senate has ever seen," Politico editor Mike DeBonis wrote on X.

National Rifle Association public affairs director and Maine native Justin Davis responded to the clip by predicting that "the upcoming debates are going to be gold." NOTUS reporter Igor Bobic, meanwhile, said that Collins used a "Trump tactic" by bringing up a subject while pretending not to mention it.

"Count Collins out (like everyone did in '20) at your own peril," Targeted Victory CCO Matt Gorman posted on X.

"Susan Collins from the top rope on Troy Jackson," GOP communicator Steve Guest posted on X.

Reports about Jackson's relationship with his second cousin first surfaced in July, when The Maine Wire reported that Jackson and his longtime partner share the same great-grandparents.

Maine Democrats Crown Troy Jackson As Platner Replacement As Fresh Scrutiny Clouds Senate Reset

"It's truly hysterical how Democrats can't seem to find one normal dude to run for office," conservative commentator Greg Price posted on X, alluding to the fact that Jackson replaced Graham Platner on the ballot in Maine after he terminated his campaign amid a rape allegation.

Other aspects of Jackson's personal life have come to the forefront of his Senate campaign, including a 1988 police report which claims he assaulted a man at a bar. The report also states that his partner accused him of pushing her around.

Jackson does not dispute that he attacked another man, but strongly denies laying a hand on his partner, who has said she does not recall giving a statement to that effect to the police.

When asked about the police report in August, Collins told Fox News Digital that "he's the one that needs to respond to the reports. I'm not going to comment on them. But I will say that based on widespread reporting it appears that he struggles to control his temper ... From my perspective, it seems that vetting is very important. We learned the failure of vetting with Graham Platner. But that's really up to the Democrats."

Embattled Maine Democrat Deadlocked With Collins Despite Controversies In Key Senate Race, New Poll Shows

During her interview with Politico, Collins denied that Jackson would necessarily be an easier opponent than Platner, pointing out that the former has a long political record that he can be criticized over — something that Platner lacked as a political outsider.

Jackson has framed the GOP focus on his personal life as a distraction from the issues Mainers actually care about.

"Susan Collins will do anything to distract from the fact that she votes with Trump 96% of the time and has sold out working people in Maine," his campaign previously told Fox News Digital. "Personal attacks on Troy's family are shameful and desperate."

The Jackson campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

Fox News Digital's Paul Steinhauser contributed to this report.

title: Number of Iranian military personnel reported killed by US strikes this week rises to 13
description: DUBAI, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency reported on Thursday the deaths of six more military personnel from U.S. strikes this week, bringing the military death toll to at
fullText:
DUBAI, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency reported on Thursday the deaths of six more military personnel from ‌U.S. strikes this week, bringing the military death toll to ‌at least 13.

The U.S. strikes on Tuesday were the most extensive for weeks. In ​the latest report on military deaths, Tasnim said six members of the regular military, including three pilots, had been killed in southern Iran. It gave no additional detail on the location.

Tasnim had earlier reported that Tuesday's ‌strikes had killed three members ⁠of the paramilitary Basij on Lavan Island in the Gulf, with their funeral taking place in southern Iran ⁠on Wednesday.

The strikes also killed four members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' (IRGC) Aerospace Force in western Iran, according to a statement by the ​guards published ​on Wednesday.

Iranian military casualties in the ​conflict that began in late ‌February have been reported periodically, without official confirmation of overall tolls.

The war, which began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, has left thousands of people dead, the vast majority of them in Iran and Lebanon.

On Wednesday, an Iranian health ministry official said on X that ‌from August 30 to September 2, 18 ​people had been killed, including four people ​attending a wedding, and ​142 had been wounded, drawing renewed attention to the ‌civilian death toll.

Tasnim has also reported ​that U.S. strikes ​on southern Iran on Sunday, which followed a month-long lull in clashes, had killed three people. Two were identified as members ​of the IRGC Navy ‌by Iran's Nournews outlet.

The U.S. has reported 18 military personnel ​killed and more than 750 wounded in the war.

title: FSU football running game may be best chance at pulling off SMU upset
description: Florida State football's first stock market is open: Three Seminoles are surging, three are slipping after the 34-17 win over New Mexico State.
fullText:
Florida State opened the 2026 season with a 34-17 victory over New Mexico State, but one game provided plenty of insight into which players are trending upward and which still have questions to answer.

While it's far too early for overreactions, the Seminoles' season opener offered an early glimpse of who's building momentum heading into Monday night's ACC showdown against SMU. From standout performances in the backfield to concerns along both lines of scrimmage, here's Florida State's first stock report of the season.

Kromah looked every bit like the feature that Florida State envisioned entering the season.

The sophomore consistently wore down New Mexico State's defense while displaying the explosiveness and elusiveness that made him one of the Seminoles' most anticipated players. He finished with 115 rushing yards on 14 carries, highlighted by a 52-yard run that helped set the tone offensively.

With high expectations surrounding him as FSU's lead back, Kromah delivered an encouraging start to the season.

Few players impacted the game in more ways than Singleton.

The versatile playmaker contributed as a runner, receiver and return specialist, totaling 164 all-purpose yards and two touchdowns. His performance earned him ACC Receiver of the Week honors on Monday.

"Sam's a guy who's a really talented football player," head coach Mike Norvell said. "He's growing, just in all areas. I was proud of him to see his impact in all three phases of it."

Singleton and Kromah already appear capable of forming one of the conference's most dynamic backfield tandems. If that continues, it should take pressure off quarterback Ashton Daniels and create more balance in Florida State's offense.

Jones' return to full strength could be one of Florida State's biggest developments on defense.

The cornerback, who spent much of the offseason working back from a season-ending injury, looked confident in coverage. He recorded a pass breakup and an interception while making several plays on deep-ball attempts.

"You've seen him grow mentally off the field, on the field now," Norvell said.

"He gets to start tonight. He has a PBU, gets the interception in the end zone. Take us through the growth from him, his mentality, and what you're going to expect from him this season."

Defensive coordinator Tony White praised Jones on Monday, noting he was among the defense's top performers in the opener. His emergence adds another playmaker to an already talented secondary.

"He's been acting right like he's the best version of himself on and off the field, and it's translated," White said.

There were understandable questions about Gbayor after an injury sidelined him throughout spring practice.

The veteran linebacker quickly eased those concerns against New Mexico State. Playing in a rotational role, Gbayor recorded four tackles and a sack while bringing physicality and energy to Florida State's defense.

His familiarity with White's 3-3-5 system, dating back to their time together at Nebraska, continues to make him a valuable piece of one of the Seminoles' deepest position groups.

Danzy's transition from running back to wide receiver appears to be taking another significant step forward.

The Tallahassee native tied Singleton for the team lead with four receptions and finished with 51 receiving yards. His best play came on a skinny post route in the first quarter that helped set up a scoring opportunity.

With Duce Robinson expected to draw considerable attention from opposing defenses, Danzy has a chance to emerge as a reliable secondary receiving option.

Florida State's offensive line remains a work in progress, but Pabst was one of its brightest spots in the opener.

The Bowling Green transfer started at right guard and even saw snaps as an extra tight end. According to Pro Football Focus, Pabst did not allow a sack or pressure across 69 snaps.

Offensive line coach Herb Hand called Pabst the unit's most consistent player before the season, and the former All-MAC lineman backed up that praise in Week 0.

After promising freshman seasons, Mandrell and Darryll Desir had relatively quiet starts to their sophomore campaigns.

Mandrell finished with four tackles, while Darryll was credited with one. More concerning was the lack of consistent pressure generated by either player as Florida State searched for disruption along the defensive front.

The Seminoles will need more production from both linemen against an SMU offense expected to present a tougher challenge.

Wisner's stock dips more because of usage than performance.

The former Texas running back was expected to be part of a three-man rotation alongside Kromah and Singleton, but he saw the fewest opportunities among the group's primary contributors. Wisner totaled 34 yards on four carries, averaging an impressive 8.5 yards per attempt.

His limited workload was one of the more surprising developments of the opener. The good news for Wisner is that one game doesn't define a season, and his role could expand as conference play begins.

Nwaiwu endured a difficult debut at right tackle.

According to Pro Football Focus, the Stephen F. Austin transfer was responsible for five pressures, the most on the team. He surrendered one sack, one quarterback hit and three hurries as New Mexico State found success attacking his side of the line.

There's still plenty of time for improvement, particularly as Nwaiwu adjusts to a higher level of competition, but his performance will be one of the areas Florida State must address before facing SMU.

title: 3 questions for Arkansas football in Week 1 against North Alabama
description: An FCS opponent at home should be a smooth season opener. Here are our three biggest questions for Arkansas football in Week 1 vs North Alabama.
fullText:
FAYETTEVILLE — It's time to see what Ryan Silverfield's first Arkansas football team looks like against an external opponent.

After competing against themselves throughout spring practices and fall camp over the last six months, the Hogs return to Razorback Stadium for the Week 1 matchup against North Alabama on Saturday, Sept. 5.

Major sportsbooks view Arkansas as a five-touchdown favorite against the FCS competition. In all likelihood, Silverfield will open his tenure with a home romp.

But the first game of a new era will still provide plenty of evaluation points for a brand new coaching staff and a roster filled with newcomers. Here are three questions we'll be closely following in this weekend's game against the Lions.

North Alabama racked up six sacks against Samford during a 22-10 victory in Week 0. A steady pass rush played a big role in a dominant defensive effort.

"They move and twist a lot," Arkansas guard Kobe Branham said about the North Alabama defensive line. "That's kind of been our emphasis this week, figuring out the keys to when they're doing it and then how they're going to do it during the game."

The task gets much larger for North Alabama, both literally and figuratively, as it shifts focus to an SEC offensive line.

However, the Razorbacks are ushering in new starters at both tackle spots and have a first-year leader under center. The season could tailspin if the offensive line proves to be a weakness. Against an FCS opponent, it's imperative that Arkansas keeps Jackson clean and gives him time in the pocket to attack down the field. The tests will become much more difficult in the coming weeks against No. 21 Utah and No. 3 Georgia.

North Alabama didn't run wild against Samford, but the Lions stayed committed with 165 yards on 47 carries. They were able to win the time-of-possession battle and tie the opposing defense.

"They have a good run game. We're excited for the challenge as a defensive line, as a defense as a whole. We're just going to come in and do what we're supposed to do," Arkansas defensive tackle Hunter Osborne said.

In Arkansas' season-opener last year, Alabama A&M's top-three running backs all averaged more than four yards per carry. It was a sign of struggles on the horizon.

Osborne, David Oke and Carlon Jones will be the three primary defenders up the middle. They'll have Quincy Rhodes and Xadavien Sims setting the edge. One year after ranking 116th nationally in rushing defense, the Hogs must set the tone on a stronger campaign in 2026.

There is quiet confidence that Arkansas has made significant upgrades at the cornerback position, but three August additions at safety should hint that the coaching staff has concerns about the back end of the secondary.

The 5-for-5 players will be eligible against North Alabama, but Silverfield isn't planning on thrusting those players into big roles in Week 1. Instead, defensive coordinator Ron Roberts said that Arkansas will primarily rely on a three-man rotation at safety comprised of Christian Harrison, Miguel Mitchell and Kyeaure Magloire.

It would be a positive sign if that trio can have a strong opening game. The middle of the field was too often a vulnerability for the 2025 Razorbacks, and that included pour passing defense from the linebacker room. If Arkansas is going to field a much-improved defense this fall, these two positions will need to be better in coverage.

Jackson Fuller covers Arkansas football, basketball and baseball for the Southwest Times Record, part of the USA TODAY Network. Reach him at jfuller@usatodayco.com or follow him @jacksonfuller16 on X, formerly known as Twitter.

fullText:
The Georgia Bulldogs host their first Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS) opponent in Week 2 of the college football season. Georgia plays the Western Kentucky Hilltoppers on Saturday, Sept. 12 at 12:45 p.m. ET.

Against the Hilltoppers, Georgia is debuting an all-white uniform combination. Georgia has always had white jerseys, but the Dawgs typically wear silver britches and red helmets. Against Western Kentucky, Georgia will wear white helmets and white pants. Recruits have commonly worn the all-white uniforms on visits, but Georgia has never won them in a game. That changes against Western Kentucky.

Georgia opens the season against Tennessee State at home, while Western Kentucky plays at Nevada in Week 1. The Hilltoppers are expected to start Rodney Tisdale Jr. at quarterback. Tisdale passed for 1,432 yards and had 11 total touchdowns in 2025.

Western Kentucky will be Georgia's final tune up game before the Bulldogs begin a stretch of playing nine straight SEC opponents. Georgia's SEC opener is on the road against Arkansas in Week 3 on Sept. 19.

The Bulldogs are 1-0 in series history against Western Kentucky. Georgia won the only meeting 48-12 back in 2006.
